Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the House to-morrow go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to make provision for the improvement and management of the Harbour of Three Rivers, in the province of Quebec, and to provide:
1.	That the Commissioners appointed under this act shall be incorporated under the name of the "Three Rivers Harbour Commissioners".
2.	That boundaries of the harbour be defined; harbour commissioners and a harbour master, a deputy harbour master and other officers be appointed; and rules and regulations, and a tariff of rates and dues be made.
3.	That the jurisdiction of the commissioners be defined, as well as their powers as to expropriation of lands and the making of by-laws, the collection of rents, and the borrowing of money.
4.	That the commissioners shall expend the moneys collected, after payment of the salary of the harbour master and the necessary expenses of maintenance of the harbour, in improving the harbour and its appurtenances, according to plans to be approved by the minister.
5.	That regulations as to seizures, penalties, the application of the same, and the general administration of the harbour be established.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General having been informed of the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the consideration of the House.
Motion agreed to.

SAINT JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the provisions of chapter 12 of the statutes of 1921, be amended by extending the time for the completion of the Saint John and Quebec Railway between Centreville, in the county of Carleton, and Andover, in the county of Victoria, New Brunswick, from the 31st day of December, 1923, to 31st day of December, 1925.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Why is this resolution
necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It involves a subsidy,
and my legal instructions are that as the proposed amendment to the act contemplates the payment of money on the completion of the work a resolution is necessary.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

The minister
might tell us how the work stands, how much has been constructed and how much remains to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There is a stretch of
twenty-six miles on this road on which there has not been any construction. This portion of the line, in fact the entire line, was undertaken under an agreement between the provincial government of New Brunswick and the federal government in 1916. In 1919, an act was passed extending the time for completion to 1921, and in 1921 an act was again passed extending the time until 1923. The purpose of the present resolution is to extend it for a further period until 1925. As a matter of fact no work has been done on this twenty-six miles. I understand that both the people and the legislature of New Brunswick are very anxious that we should extend the time for the completion of the work for another two years. If the matter were merely an extension of time for the charter the bill would no doubt go through the Railway committee in the ordinary course; but it involves a subsidy and this procedure has been followed in connection with the two previous extensions.

What is the
status of the company now? Is the road owned by the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The St. John Railwav
is owned by the province but operated by the Canadian National Railways under an agreement; the province of New Brunswick has the fixed charges while the Canadian

St. John and Quebec Railway
National Railways carry on the operation. I regret to say that no money is being made.

The company is really an
artificial concern; it is the province of New Brunswick. I believe that the railway is still owned in a perfectly nominal way by the company, but it is really the province that is involved.
Mr. MARC1L (Bonaventure):	Is it paying?

Is any railway paying? This matter is one in regard to which I should like to have some further information if possible. For some time the process which the minister has referred to has been carried on, that is to say, the extending of the charter by provincial legislation and the subsidy by Dominion legislation. Has the minister any definite, concrete proposal from the provincial authorities with regard to the completion of this very much needed portion of the road? Or is the whole matter simply in the uncertain state which the minister implies, pending the dawn of some happy day when the work may be taken up in earnest? 1 am not going to enter into a discussion of what has been considered on the floor of this house many times as to the routing of the Transcontinental railway through New Brunswick. The Transcontinental railway, so far as it passes through New Brunswick, is a completed fact. The province assumed the burden of building the Valley railway because that railway was needed to do the work that many of us thought ought to have been done by the Transcontinental. Unfortunately, the Transcontinental was connected from Grand Falls to Moncton by practically a straight road through territory which will never produce much traffic, and the St. John valley has been left aside by every government since confederation. At the time of confederation the Intercolonial was built on the extreme northern and eastern side of the province because of a military bugbear. The Transcontinental, for some unknown purpose, was run to Moncton, as if it were possible io create a winter port there; and the route of the St. John valley, one of the most fertile parts of the province and one that requires connection to the greatest extent, was left unserved except in so far as it was served by the purely local Canadian Pacific railway line. The gap which this resolution deals with would enable the St. John Valley railway to be connected with the Transcontinental at a much better junction than now exists. In other words, it would connect at one end with the Transcontinental, which would then be able to use the St. 
John railway throughout its entire length, instead of stopping halfway at Fredericton as is now the case, and using the line between Fredericton and St. John. I think, despite the fact that we do not want to have any additions to the public debt that can possibly be avoided, it would be well worth while for the government-or, I suppose, it is now the Railway board-to take this matter up in earnest with the idea of lifting the burden off the province of New Brunswick,| a burden which that province was compelled to assume because provision had not been made otherwise for this absolutely necessary routing. If this road were completed and made part of the government system the whole burden would be taken off the province. Besides it would then be much easier to reach the port of St. John, as well as the port of Halifax, with western freight, because the gradients would be easier and the distance from Montreal to St. John not any longer than, if as long as, from Montreal to Portland, Maine. To us in the Martime provinces this is a very important question. I notice that in some newspapers, published not very far from the city of Ottawa, we are constantly being reminded that the Maritime provinces should not make requests for lower freight rates or further railway facilities. Apparently we ought to be "good little boys" down there and put up with existing conditions. We, however, inspired by other examples in this House, propose to reiterate our case just as frequently as we can get an opportunity to do so; and perhaps repeated importunity may on some government at some time have the effect that repeated importunity is said to have had upon a certain person very much worse in reputation than the present or any past government. Speaking with all seriousness, I do not think that the million or million and a half that might be involved in completing this work would be at all a burden upon the National Railway system, but such expenditure would remove an encumbrance which the railway system is placing to-day both upon the province and upon the Dominion. That is one way of making the system profitable and improving its facilities, and is above all one of the great means of utilizing a port within the Dominion instead of neglecting it to the advantage of a port lying outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
So far as we are aware, there has been no definite proposition recently for the construction of these twenty-six miles, although the Premier of New Brunswick has written an urgent letter that this act be extended for another two years in the hope that

St. John and Quebec Railway
some arrangement may be arrived at before the expiration of that time.

As this is a matter not with a private railway company which is seeking to get its charter extended from time to time, but really with the province, why not put the legislation on the statute books in such a wav that it will always be open to be taken advantage of by the province? Why limit the province to two years, why not keep the thing perpetually open?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I imagine the province itself will renew the charter to this company every two years.
They might as well renew it for an indefinite period.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If the subsidy keeps up with the renewal of the charter it is doing pretty well. Except under special act, no charter is extended for more than two years under the Railway Act, and the subsidy generally follows the extension of time for the completion of the road.

But the minister realizes that this is not a private railway company. Although it is under the name of the St. John and Quebec Railway Company, it is really the province of New Brunswick and nobody else, and you might just as well deal with the matter under the name of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: You could not do that.

Why have the province of
New Brunswick secured legislation here every two years to extend the right to get this subsidy? Or why have them go through the farce every year of themselves passing legislation to complete this railway? Why not enact legislation providing that the provincial government may complete this road whenever it sees fit, and that then the federal government will come to its aid to the amount promised? Why load up our statute books every two years with a mere farcical proceeding like this when one government is dealing with another, not with some private railway company which perhaps is trying to get an undue extension of some right which others would like to avail themselves of?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Legally it is a private company we are dealing with, although the province of New Brunswick, I suppose, owns the controlling interest.
It does.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That company, by agreement with the province of New Brunswick,
might transfer the right to some other company.
Not without the consent of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
But without our consent. Then we would be extending for all eternity a subsidy to a private railway company. I think some safeguard ought to be applied to these charters without exception, because parliament is always reasonable in extending the time for completion of the project when reasonable grounds are shown therefor.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Graham thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 191 to authorize an extension of the time for the completion of the Saint John and Quebec Railway between Centreville, in the county of Carleton, and Andover, in the county of Victoria, N.B.

One item under this vote is "Canadian National Parks and Historic Sites, $1,250,980," and in connection with that item I would like to bring to the minister's attention the historic site of Fort Edward, formerly the Indian Fort Pisiquid, in the town of Windsor. Last year, through neglect, the old block house on this site was burned down, and the site generally is being permitted to go to waste. I believe the minister has appointed a caretaker for it, but it is practically a case of locking the barn door after the horse is stolen. This is one of the most ancient forts in Nova Scotia, and I do not believe it should be under the Parks branch; I should like to see it under the Quebec Battlefields Commission if at all possible, because they do things in more proper style and more in accordance with what the people demand. At present the Parks Commission exists absolutely for the purpose of keeping up certain things in the prairie provinces, such as Jasper Park or the buffalo park at Wainwright, and the like. Now, we in Nova Scotia have many historic sites, one of the most interesting of which is right in the shire town of the county which I have the honour to represent. It is a place that was used in days gone by to enable the English soldiers to defend themselves and the people against the attacks of the Indians. I believe that the people of the province of Quebec have a proper sense of sentiment, and that sentiment is equally pronounced in the people of the Maritime provinces. The keeping up of these areas in the western provinces is purely a matter of dollars and cents; it is a matter which is entirely devoid of sentiment. As Sir Ernest Shackleton once said, "You may call it sentiment if you will, but the world sadly needs sentiment." There should be some sentiment as regards these historic sites in Nova Scotia, and I would like to ask the minister if it would not be possible to have the ancient site of Fort Edward placed under the control , of the Quebec Battlefields Commission.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not very much information with respect to the Quebec Battlefields

Commission, but I do know that the Historic Sites Commission have been sitting for some time, and taking into consideration the merits of the various historic sites throughout Canada with a view to preserving them and keeping them in repair.
Who are the representatives of Nova Scotia on the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: E. Plimsoll Edwards of Halifax.

I know Dr. Edwards very well indeed; he is one of the most important officials of the Nova Scotia Historical Society But the way they proceed is to put a brass tablet on some old building and then let it go to pieces. That is what the Nova Scotia Historical Society is doing at the present time-of course, they also have a few papers read. I suggest that a fence be put around the portion of the site containing the remnants of the blockhouse, and the old fort, and that repairs be carried out as far as possible; of course, the minister cannot by modern methods restore an old site to. its original condition. I suggest also that the rest of the ground be set aside as a playground for the town where the children could be inspired with something of the sentiment of what their ancestors did. During the late war these grounds were used by the 112th Battalion, which was commanded by an esteemed friend of mine, though a political opponent, Colonel Tremain, and other battalions from various sections of Canada were quartered there. Let us do what we can to inculcate a proper sentiment in the minds of the people rather than a love of dollars and cents, which is all too prevalent to-day in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
All I can say in reply to my hon. friend is that the matter he complains of has been discussed
4 p.m. by the Historic Sites Commission and they intend to take action to preserve this site and keep it in order.

But has the minister considered, or will this committee consider, the advisability of placing this historic site under the Quebec Battlefields Commission? I believe that is its name, but call it what you will, I believe it has more idea of doing what the people of Canada desire than the Historic Sites Commission has. And will the minister also consider the advisability of permitting that portion of the land which is not used for the purposes of the historic site to be set aside as a playground for the children?

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know very much about the activities of the Quebec commission. I do know, however, of the work of the commission that has recently been appointed to deal with these sites. There are many historic sites in Canada that the people are desirous of having marked and preserved, and there is a considerable amount of work for this organization. As to the advisability of handing the site he mentions over to the Quebec commission, I cannot give my hon. friend a. definite answer as to that at the moment.

I do not think the Historic Sites Commission are conversant with what these sites represent to the people locally. Fort Edward, or the Indian Fort Pisiquid, which was the Indian name of the shire town of my constituency, is a site of great historic value to every person in Nova Scotia, and particularly the people in the county of Hants. I should like to see adopted, as regards that site, the same rules and regulations as are adopted by the Quebec Battlefields Commission. If the site is not placed under the control of that commission, I should like to see it administered as the Quebec Battlefields Commission administer sites which come under their control. About two and a half acres will be sufficient to enclose the actual historic site, that is, the partly destroyed block house and the old fort as it stands. For many years it has been requested that the land be allocated to the local commission in the town of Windsor, who would be under the control of the representatives of the government there, or of the caretaker, and that the area not fenced in should be used as a playground, for toboggan slides, for camping areas, for the Boy Scouts, and so on. This would result in benefit to the children; it would encourage a proper sentiment, and would help out the Defence department, all at comparatively small expense to the country. I am not asking for anything new. If the right hon. the leader of the Opposition will consult the Minister of Militia of his day he will ascertain that petitions asking for this were received at that time from the town of Windsor-that is, prior to the time this government came into power, and prior to my election for this constituency. Many of the men who are advocating this are political opponents of mine, but I think they are actuated by a desire to see that ample ground should be given to the children of the locality to play in, and where they will be under proper supervision. This fort is right in the heart of the town, the land has an area of twenty-eight acres, and at present it is not used for any
purpose. That, I think, is absolutely absurd when this land could be made to serve some useful end. If the children could use this land as a playground under the supervision of the caretaker, the historic associations would tend to inspire them with greater love for their ancestors and their surroundings. Not only that, but the children could there indulge in exercises calculated to develop their physique. If, owing to the influence of red tape, this historic site is retained as it is the children of the neighbourhood will derive no benefit whatever. Let me say, in conclusion, that I intend to keep pressing this matter until I get a definite promise, and not a mere evasive answer, in regard to this particular piece of ground.
I rather dissent from the expressions uttered by the hon. member and am a little surprised to hear that the province of Nova Scotia enjoys a monopoly in the matter of Canadian sentiment.

Canadian sentiment?
What has it to do with Canadian sentiment?
I should like to ask my hon. friend if he considers the preservation of the great herds of buffalo at Wainwright park is a mere matter of dollars and cents?

I may tell my hon. friend that I am not opposing in any way the preservation of the great herds of buffalo at Wain-wright park. Do that if you want to, but do not maintain playgrounds out there, which are invaded by tourists, from the mere standpoint of making dollars and cents. We are not asking for such a thing as that. We are asking for the preservation of our historic sites in the province of Nova Scotia. We are asking that this site in the town of Windsor shall be given, under proper supervision, to the town as a place where the children can play.

I think my hon. friend
from Hants is quite right. I sympathize with him in his determination not to be buffaloed in any way out of his historic site.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry the impression should have been created that I was trying to buffalo anybody out of his historic site. If my hon. friend (Mr. Martell) will make it clear that the town of Windsor is prepared to maintain and take care of the land granted to them there would be absolutely no objection so far as I am concerned, provided a sufficient area is fenced off and preserved as an historic site.

I notice in connection with the item of Canadian National parks and historical sites an increase of $284,480 for this year. The minister will recall that I have asked that some consideration should be given to the question of improvements in connection with a pleasure resort in my own district. In making this request let me remind the committee that this is the first occasion this session that I have asked for any concession or any privilege from the government. The need of these improvements has been repeatedly urged not only upon the present administration but upon previous governments. Prior to 1911 the desired work was commenced. It was cancelled after the change of government took place in 1911. The need for this work is just as pressing now as it ever was. I am speaking of the Moose mountains in the district of Assiniboia. We have there five lakes of perhaps six or seven hundred acres in extent, and the towns have expended quite a sum of money in endeavouring to make the spot a pleasure resort for the people of the neighbourhood. I may inform the committee that White Bear lake and Fish lake constitute a rendezvous for hundreds, yes thousands, of visitors who come from the United States. I recall a statement by the leader of the Opposition to the effect that our parks in western Canada formed a source of revenue equal to the agricultural area. I quite believe that statement is true. The Moose mountains resort is far removed from any other place of the kind; it might serve as a stepping stone, if the expression is permissible, to tourists as they proceed through the West in connection with the programme for national road construction on which we are engaged at the present time. I am sure it would be a great source of revenue if the resort in question were further developed. I have in my possession at the present time some beautiful pictures that were taken in the western part of Alberta and the Rocky mountains, but I do not think I err in stating that you can get just as good pictures from scenes in the Moose mountains. I do not think it would involve a very large expenditure on the part of the Dominion government to carry out the necessary improvements. If a road were built around the two lakes referred to, White Bear lake and Fish lake, it would enable tourists to reach those lovely valleys and mountains and view scenery of the most beautiful description. I often have the opportunity of visiting those lakes and I can speak from experience of the 
magnificent scenery which unfolds itself to view. Tourists from British Columbia come to the Moose mountains. In their own province they have scenery of the finest description, but if they leave that and come to the Moose mountains, as they do, it is surely a great tribute to the natural beauties of that district. I earnestly press upon the minister the desirability of giving this matter his best consideration.

Grant to Canadian Forestry Association, $4,000.
May I ask why this amount is decreased? It was $8,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Formerly,
$4,000 was the amount granted to the Canadian Forestry Association. As my hon. friend will see, there is a considerable increase in our forestry vote which we have just passed, and it is becoming increasingly difficult to prevent forest fires-at least it has been in the past few years. I am hoping that the moisture they get in western Canada will make the work less difficult, but we must admit the loss of a tremendous amount of timber. However, comparing the losses of the Dominion forest reserves with that of the provinces, it has not been so severe, because Canada as a whole had a tremendous loss. We were somewhat fortunate, perhaps, in not suffering so much by fire in the three prairie provinces and in the forests in British Columbia. This Forestry Association is doing a very great work. It was instituted by people interested in forestry protection, the manufacturers of lumber and kindred products. For years, as far as I can ascertain, they received a grant of $4,000. They seem to have increased their activities and asked for an increased grant.
The Forestry branch of the department is organized, I think, on very good lines and is prepared to do a splendid work in propagating knowledge with respect to forest fires generally. Perhaps we are weak in not having technically trained men to combat forest diseases. If we are weak in one branch, it is that particular branch. I think we should have entomologists to deal with that question, because it is rather a serious one. Outside of that, we have a splendid organization, prepared to disseminate the information we obtain, which we propose to do through the different schools. I feel that, inasmuch as we are prepared to do directly through the department the class of work that was undertaken by the Forestry Association, we might very well revert to the old grant to this association, and expend the money under our supervision, because I think we can do it as cheaply, and perhaps just as well, and in fact I think very much better, than they have been able to do. I am not for a single moment decrying the -work this organization has done. They have gone through the country with a car and by lectures interested the people in forest preservation and the prevention of fires, while our work is more of the character of actually extinguishing fires when started. So that on the whole, I think if we revert to the old grant which this association has been receiving, and use the balance for the purpose of carrying on propaganda to educate the children, and adults as well, against carelessness with respect to fires which destroy timber that is valuable, it might be beneficial. I think I am safe in saying that more timber has been destroyed by fire than has been actually cut. That is a serious situation, and we hope in the forestry department to do our utmost to assist in abating this destruction. That is the reason for the reduction in the grant.

In regard to forest fires, it has always seemed to me that if this government could pass legislation under which they could conscript the people in the vicinity of the fire, and pay them not more than a dollar a day to fight the fire, our loss through forest fires would be reduced. I have noticed, particularly in haying time in my own district *-and I make the statement in this House without hesitation-that more fires are started to get people employment than in any other way. They get bigger wages than the farmers can pay for haying and such work. I have known the men to be taken out of the hay fields to fight fires. The Forestry department would pay a third more than we were able to pay them for making hay. I think if there
Supply-Interior

were a law passed and people conscripted in the district where the fire was and paid as I have already said not more than one dollar a day it would cause everybody to take an interest in keeping the fires down.
