speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Forestry Conference is a conference that was started in 1920, the outcome of a meeting in London. It embraces the whole of the overseas dominions as well as Great Britain. It is for the purpose of studying more intimately forestry matters. I believe it was well under way under the regime of the Hon. Sir James Lougheed, and that Canada was offered the conference for 1923. I know that as soon as I came into office the matter came up actively, and I believed it was of sufficient importance to the people of Canada to have representatives from all the overseas dominions come here and hold a conference, because not only will they hold a conference in Canada, but they will travel through Canada and so be-

Supply-Interior
come more familiar with our forest wealth, and, perhaps, this will dissipate some of the delusions held particularly by overseas people with respect to our timber. Hon. gentlemen will remember that for a considerable period, during the war, notwithstanding the fact that we have splendid spruce timber that can be manufactured for almost any purpose for which that timber is used, a great deal was brought from the United States. I felt it would be good business to bring to Canada these outstanding forestry men from the overseas dominions, and also English people who are interested, and let them see what we have in the way of forest wealth. Moreover, it would give us a better understanding, as well as assisting our officials and others interested in reforestation and kindred subjects, to hold a conference of this kind in Canada.

I suppose the minister is aware of the fact that a large quantity of timber is imported from the United States, for binder tongues, seeder tongues, and nearly all farm implement tongues. We have no timber of that kind suitable for the purpose. I believe it is Georgia pine, red pine I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know what my hon. friend has in mind, Georgia pine, which is used for the construction of tongues, shafts and that sort of thing. It is a very tough wood. So far as I know, we have nothing to compare with it in Canada.
I think it is pretty poor stuff.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Manufacturers of farm implements must pay more for it than for our Douglas pine. On my farm, when I had a breakdown, I usually substituted by putting in 4 x 4 Douglas fir rather than by buying a new binder pole from the company. We got fairly good satisfaction, with the single exception that the fir, as hon. members know, does not stand the sun very well and will warp considerably. We are giving consideration to matters of that kind in the laboratory of our Forestry branch.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The size of this grant, $30,000, is accounted for by the fact that the conference is to be in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To pay for the conference, yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not know how far the matter proceeded under my successor, but I do not think it would have proceeded very far had I been in the department myself. I think the whole conference matter is overdone. In the Interior department scarcely a week went by that a call for a conference
was not worked up and presented to thef minister in most plausible form. The salvation of the country was to depend upon the sending of some of the officials of the department here, there and everywhere, chasing after conferences and information. I do not want to stand as one who deprecates the education of our foresters in the very best methods that any country in the world can produce. If there is a country that requires the best forestry service it is Canada. I am not reflecting in the least degree on the efficiency of our forestry organization, because I should have had to give more concentrated attention to it and travel more to examine it than I was able to do to assure myself that it was a thorough organization; but I have no reason to say that it was not; that is all I can say. I should think, however, that the publications of foresters the world over, the scientific works that are available to all members of our forestry service, and the literature that exists on the subject and which is by no means sparse, would be all that was required to bring the latest ideas to the attention of the men of our own force. Why it is necessary for somebody in China to come face to face with somebody in Brazil and be met there by somebody else from Sweden, together with all the fraternity of foresters from every part of the world, to hold a jubilee in order that they might get one another's opinions, I never could understand.
And at great expense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The fact is that it is not at their own expense, and the temptation is very great for them to hold such conferences. And, inasmuch as there is an object to be attained, human nature is such that they can readily and honestly convince themselves that it is a splendid thing to do and all to the advantage of the country. I do not think that this item should be here and I commit myself to that position even though preparations for the conference may have been under way under Sir James Lougheed. I was not aware myself that they were under way, but I think the minister would have been well advised to let the honour pass by, and let them hold the conference somewhere else. Possibly a representative of the department could attend to see whether we could get any advantage from it before making a large commitment. Speaking generally, not with any special reference to forestry, but with as much reference to twenty or thirty other branches of the service, I offer in all humility this advice to the minister and to the government: Be on guard against propaganda for conferences.
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Inasmuch as there is a very strong desire in British Columbia to introduce their timber, of which they have a great deal, into New Zealand, for example, as well as the desire for inter-empire trade, I felt that this particular conference might be of some value in the way of spreading a knowledge of Canada's timber resources. In the main, I agree with the hon. gentleman in what he says in reference to conferences. Frankly, I confess that I am not personally very much enamoured of the results to be obtained from conferences, and perhaps we are going entirely too far with an expenditure of this character. But this matter apparently was settled; the offer had been made to Canada and to some extent had been accepted. I do think that the conference will serve to dissipate a great deal of misapprehension in regard to our forest products, and, further, will undoutedly be of advantage to the people who have to do with our forests. I know of no part of our public resources that stands in greater need of proper methods of preservation than does our forest wealth. We have a vast wealth there if we can only preserve it from fire. The insect danger is not so serious; but fire is unquestionably responsible for losses that run into millions annually. While I can assure the committee that I shall not, while I am in charge of the Department of Interior, come back for large votes for forestry conventions, I do think at the same time that if we cannot adequately combat the fire menace with the present force we shall have to extend it. It would pay the people of Canada greatly to extend the force, because the cost of the Forestry branch is a very small item indeed in comparison with the tremendous .losses we suffer annually.
Are we following any systematic plan of reforestation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. There are stations at the following places: Spruce Woods, Duck Mountain, Riding Mountain, Mute Mountain, in Manitoba; Nisbet, Beaver Hills and Pines in Saskatchewan; Cypress and Cooking Lake in Alberta.

Has there been any recognition of any sort of the work of Mr. Bamjum for the work he has been doing in this connection? As far as I am able to judge, he appears to be rendering a great patriotic service in drawing the attention of the public to the widespread destruction of our forests by the spruce bud worm and other pests.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is the member not
aware that in the budget the government promised a royal commission to Mr. Bamjum to look into the question he had raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend asks if we are going to give him any remuneration?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Any recognition.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I presume
he meant in the way of remuneration. Mr. Bamjum ge'ts a great deal of recognition- he is considered an authority on the subject. At the moment he is advocating the prohibition of the export of pulp wood as a means of conserving our forest wealth. Of course, there is conservation on all the Crown lands-no wood goes out of Canada except that which is cut off private lands.

Mr. Barnjum is drawing
the attention of the public to the fact that millions and millions of feet of timber is being lost to Canada annually by the destruction of the spruce bud worm.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend from Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) gave us an address on that subject last session. I had that in mind when I was speaking just now.

I do not think I shall be
betraying any confidence when I say that Mr. Bamjum told me he was getting far more pleasure out of spending his money to further forest conservation than he ever got when making it. Would the minister tell us what are the activities of the Dominion government in regard to tree planting in the prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Tree planting stations are established for the purpose of furnishing trees to those requiring them. I think my honourable friend is familiar with the regulations under which trees are distributed?
That is, from the experimental farms?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, from
our tree planting stations at Indian Head and Sutherland. There has been no change of methods. I have some knowledge of the way it works out from actual experience, and I think one has only to travel through the Saskatoon district to notice the improvement in that area due to tree planting. Application is made for the trees and they are furnished as far as possible. As far as I know we have been able to supply the demand.

Supply-Interior

Could the minister
give the committee any information as to the extent or success of reforestation in the Turtle Mountain reserve in Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My information is that the trees planted there are doing well. I think I discussed that matter with Mr. Ward, the member, who seems to be very much interested.

No, Mr. Steedsman is the
member.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I beg his
pardon. He has asked us to extend the area very largely owing to the success of the first experiment.

I have heard the statement made on fairly strong authority-at least, by. a man who claimed he had knowledge of the fact-that it was the intention of the government to shortly bring in legislation prohibiting the export of pulp wood from private lands, which is going on in some of the provinces to-day. So far as I am concerned, and I have given some thought to the matter, I think it would be very good legislation. I should like to know if there is any intention on the part of the government to deal with it this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can
hardly speak with authority in a matter of this kind. Strong representations have been made to the government to prohibit the export of pulp wood, and the matter has been discussed. Considerable opposition to sucn a proposal is coming from areas in which perhaps most of the pulp wood is cut which is sent across the boundary, that is, from Quebec and New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister seems to
have forgotten the government's policy on this subject. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) announced that they would appoint a royal commission to look into the matter. So the government could not possibly make up its mind until it got the report of the commission. What has been the result of the three weeks' deliberations since that policy was announced? Has the government made any progress towards selecting the members of the commission, and what are the chances of Mr. W. T. R. Preston being chosen?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Is he applying for a position on the commission?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He always applies.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
Would the minister be
favourably inclined to extending the field of operations of the tree planting stations? I know that requests have been made by those laying out memorial parks-and I suppose other parks-for shrubs and trees, but, as the minister knows, the regulations forbid the distribution of trees for this purpose; those living in towns are not supplied.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I visited the station at Indian Head last year, and I found that most of the trees there have been required by farmers. Inasmuch as farm locations are somewhat isolated on the prairies, I think the first work of the Tree planting division should be to supply all the farmers who require trees for shelter belts around their homes, besides, these trees add very much to the appearance of the whole country. People living in towns have a great deal more protection than those in the rural districts. I would not say that it might not be advisable to extend the distribution of trees for the planting of public playgrounds, but we do not propose to make this extension for the present.

At present, even though
there is a demand for all the trees that are grown at these stations, there are times when they have a surplus of certain varieties, it being hard to gauge the exact number to be grown to meet the needs of the country. I suppose there would be no objection to these surplus trees being used for town parks?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If we had
these surpluses I would not be averse to giving them for public parks in urban centres.
Cemeteries and Parks?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am told
on the authority of one of my officers that the town of Davidson in Saskatchewan did get some trees from us for its cemetery.

I concur in the view expressed by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that this grant of 830,000 to the Empire Forestry Conference might well be dispensed with. These conferences are of doubtful value, and certainly I think a forestry conference may be of little, if any, value. I would much prefer to see the minister, instead of yielding to this departmental pressure, continue the grant to the Canadian Forestry Association. This is a voluntary organization with an advisory council representative of every province. It carries on a very valuable educational work not only

Supply-Interior

among the adult population but among the yonger generation. I presume that the minister has cut down the grant to $4,000 at the request of the association; I do not know. I think, however, that private effort in the direction undertaken by the Forestry Association with grants which it receives from this government and from some of the provincial governments and various private donors has been of a very valuable character, and it is work which I believe cannot be as successfully carried on by any department of government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Will my hon. friend explain why?
Because the gentlemen engaged in this work are actuated by their desire to render some public service. Nobody is being paid; it is entirely a voluntary undertaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The secretary is drawing a very nice salary.

That may be true; you have to pay someone to do that work. But outside of that there is very much work being undertaken that is not paid for at all. For instance, in one of the high schools in Calgary some of the gentlemen who were interested in this organization called a meeting of the parents _ and children and gave them a very valuable lecture on tree growing, tree preservation and the various methods of fire prevention. It is a voluntary effort, except so far as the central organization is concerned. In addition, they have a very excellent magazine which deals with all problems in connection with forestation. It seems to me that that work can be much better done by this private, voluntary organization than by government with a very heavy establishment, the members of which are all too anxious, perhaps, to magnify the importance of their own individual tasks. Mind you, I am not suggesting that the government's work in this connection is not important; it is a matter of vital importance to this country. But I do not think the government in undertaking this work should discourage any voluntary organization which is equally desirous of promoting the preservation of our forests in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Both in Alberta and since coming to Ottawa I have discovered that all these organizations which receive grants from the government are in many ways doing work that is government work-or if we are not doing it, we should be. I do not think that officials of the government could go into the public schools and deliver lectures on

tree planting, but they could very well send throughout the country a car equipped as the car of the Canadian Forestry Association was equipped, demonstrating proper methods of tree planting, the effects of forest fires and methods of prevention, and so on. We are actually doing that work; we have to perform the service, and we can speak authoritatively about it. As I have said, I do not for a moment wish to decry the work of this organization. But for years they have got along with this particular grant, and the tendency of all organizations receiving these grants-organizations which are outside the control of the government-is to ask for increased amounts year after year. My experience has been that once you encourage a grant of this character-not particularly this one, but any similar grant- you make it about the easiest source of their getting money. I do not know that private individuals with a desire to serve are supporting this organization and that it is doing good work. Of course, the organization was started by people who were directly interested in the preservation of the forests-there is no doubt about that-and their propaganda is undoubtedly of value. But I do think that the grant we are making might very well be continued. Only for two years did they get an increase.
I am quite prepared to stand by the
5 p.m. grant given them. The men who supported them in the past will no doubt be quite prepared to support them in the future.

I think there is a great deal in what the minister says about grants and subsidies and the evils to follow from continuing the giving of them. Frankly, for my part, I would be glad to see all that form of subsidization cut out. But since you are going to have it; since you are going to subsidize such things, we will say, as the West Indies steam packet company or the Alpine Club-and the latter is one of the most absurd grants, I think, in the estimates-we can surely afford, if we admit the principle, to continue to give a fairly reasonable grant to an association that is doing such splendid work as the Canadian Forestry Association. I am sorry the minister has economized at the expense of this association in particular. Why not economize on the Alpine Club grant and give the money to something more useful?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Alpine Club was always a theme upon which there was a very bitter controversy in our province. I suppose they do valuable work-I am not an expert on the mountain business, but I have

Supply-Interior
no doubt they render some service. But I wish to say again that I do not desire to decry the services of this forestry organization. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) is right when he says that governments might very well curtail grants of this character that go outside their control.
Do away with all of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am quite prepared to consider it.
Do not cut a good one and leave the bad one.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is a matter of judgment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I may say I approve
of both these grants-I mean, the Alpine Club and this one; I do not approve of the 330,000 conference. The Canadian Forestry Association represents men in Canada who are financially interested in the preservation of the forest, and they rightly feel that upon rhem a special responsibility rests. I presume there is a measure of altruism in their action; they are doing it for the benefit of the country, but they are doing it mainly for their own benefit. They are doing it in order that they may create a sentiment which will reflect itself in a diminished forest desolation, and in that way preserve their own property. In doing so, whether that is the motive that animates them or not does not matter, they do serve the state, because just to the degree that they prevent fires anywhere they ward off danger to government property. Not only do they serve the state in preventing fires that would consume government property, but when they preserve their own property they serve the state, because the state suffers if their property is destroyed. Consequently it seems to me that the work they are doing is a necessary work, and as we are interested in it, it is only right that we should help it; it is only right that we should contribute to any measure to encourage them, because we get to a large degree the benefit of the results of their outlay and their work. The same words really apply to the little vote to the Alpine Club. But in the absence of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and the other gallant fighter across the way who season in and season out, did brave battle in this House against that $1,000 grant, really I would not want to win the conflict by default this afternoon. I think I should wait until the enemy arrives, and then we can fight it out once more. I notice, however, that their ardour is very much cooled with the change of government.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
They have climbed
higher.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know that there is much difference as between the $8,000 and the $4,000; if the association feels that it is leceiving adequate recognition at the hands of the government when it gets $4,000, all right. I would not, however, object to a grant of $8,000.

I wish to draw the
minister's attention to a very important feature of this tree planting situation. The minister is aware that we have in the southern parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta what we term the semi-arid belt. During the last year of two there have grown up in that southern area tree planting associations the purpose of which is to induce farmers to plant and care for at least one-half mile of trees. I merely mention this matter because I believe we could in this way alter the conditions in southern Alberta and Saskatchewan; so that it is desirable that as many trees be planted there as possible. I trust that during the coming year the minister will consider carefully this phase of the situation. It is true that on the bare prairies we have planted shelter belts of trees, but these protect only the buildings. It seems to me that if that country is ever going to be saved for any useful purpose to Canada we will have to plant large areas with trees, and if we can encourage the farmers to put, say, half a mile of plantation on their farm, I fancy we will solve the problem that awaits solution in that particular area.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to say a word in endorsement of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner), and in doing so to try and press again upon the government the importance of this forest preservation question. As I find one member of the cabinet has forgotten the government policy on the subject, I really fear that its members as a whole are not very much concentrated at the present time on the subject of forest preservation. It is something very easy to make a mountain of, but as it stands it really is a problem quite difficult of solution. There are many things in my judgment that are needed. We should have a single and well-systematized Dominion organization for fighting forest fires, and this vote is rather a contribution to that end. I believe it is true that the federal organization has succeeded better than the provincial organizations. For myself, I would like to see some arrangement made by which the whole responsibility might be assumed by the federal organization. I

Supply-Interior
would like to see that done, because I am thoroughly convinced the work could be more economically and more efficiently performed under a Dominion-wide organization than it is now, distributed as it is over nine or ten organizations or more.
There must at the same time be a really more effective attack made upon the disease element of the danger. From what I can learn this has grown in peril at a prodigious rate during the last few years, attacking particularly our pine and our spruce. Just how the government is prepared to do battle against this menace I do not know. I would like the minister to explain what is really being done to protect our forests against the spruce bud worm, and against other invasions of pests that have been most marked in the last two, three or four years. Next, being certain that all that we now have in mind is being done in this direction, there are other things, it seems to me, that are equally manifest, perhaps not equally effective, which are obviously the right things to do. First of all, in my judgment there is no excuse whatever for a continuation of the present policy of permitting our raw wood to go out of this countiy. What there is in the question that should form the subject matter of a royal commission is a mystery to me. It is not something as respects which the basic facts are unknown. Royal commissions are to inquire into facts. The facts are all known. A royal commission appointed to inquire into facts that are known and acknowledged is a mere stand-off and worse. Why does not the government act? I have heard, of course, talk of reprisals. There might be, for example, a duty put on our lumber, an embargo put on American coal, an embargo put on American cotton. Let me repeat what I said the other day. Under present circumstances

we standing on our feet and the United States standing on theirs-I do not fear any reprisal from the United States, none whatever. There are reprisals they might put on that in a very short time would be the very best thing that could happen us; and there is not one that will not bring as much injury, or more, on themselves as it would do to us. So far as any word of mine can affect the government, let me say: Do not worry about reprisals; act in the best interests of the Dominion. The United States will act in their own interests without any incitement on our part. Why raw wood on private lands, any more than on public lands, should be permitted to leave the country at the present rate when our forest reserves are already perilously small, I do not know. The minister says export is

only permitted from private lands and not from the forests that are publicly owned. Very well as long as you permit export from private lands you cannot prevent export from public lands. The one channel is utilized for both and any force of inspectors that would prevent the abuse of that channel would be so expensive as to be out of the question. Consequently I hope that this idea of a royal commission will be abandoned and that the government will come to parliament this session with a real policy. Because every session this House meets from this day on the magnitude of the forest preservation problem will grow. Its present condition is of urgent consequence to this country right now. Let me say this-and I do not pretend on this subject to feel quite so sure as I do on the other-at seems to me we should in co-operation with the provinces, try to provide- though it will diminish the immediate saleable value of our forest reserves on our private and public property-some rule whereby there shall be a tree planted for every tree cut. That does not seem to me to be very impracticable; there cannot be arguments brought to bear to show that it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it is quite practicable.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If it is practicable, it should be done without the loss of another session of parliament. Furthermore, a general policy that will get results from the suggestion of the hon. member for Medicine Hat would be exceedingly beneficial to this country. It would bring the activities of hundreds of thousands of individual farmers into the great campaign for forest growth and would, at the same time distribute the benefits of that forest growth over all portions of our forest country. Some encouragement I should think could be given to that suggestion. Possibly the provinces should take part. But whether the provinces took part or not,, even if they stood quite aside, this government and people could well afford now to plant the foundation of the future wealth and strength of our coun-rty.
Mr- GRAHAM: The question of forest preservation, as has been well said by my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) and the member for Medic:ne Hat (Mr. Gardiner), means much not only to us but our children, our grandchildren and all those who are to come after us. The older provinces have control of their forest lands. The question of preserving this wealth has been discussed in the various provinces which are blessed with forest growth, as long as I have been in public life.

Supply-Interior
341?
To my mind we are not, either provincially or otherwise, doing all we can for forest preservation. Although a good deal has been done, yet it is a sad commentary on the Dominion of Canada that year by year we have such extensive forest destruction. In the province of Ontario, in which I live, if the forest wealth had been preserved and regrown by a reforestation policy up to the limit of possibility, it would mean, from a financial standpoint, a never-ending source of financial supply. In the province of Ontario the timber sales and the rental of timber areas have been a prolific source of revenue, but instead of replanting being continually working under the operation of the regrowth of a crop, that we have been decimating, we have continued to cut down our forest wealth till it has-I will not say it has all disappeared, but it is receding very rapidly. From the financial standpoint, if from no other, in our provinces, I believe it is absolutely necessary, as my right Ron. friend has said, to have every tree that is taken down replaced by another. That is done in some countries. I have been trying to recall where it is done.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Norway.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: France.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That is as to the forest, of which I will speak in a moment. Now, as to the more scattered timber throughout our farming areas-where there have been trees in years gone by, their value was not appreciated by the settlers in many cases. The moisture of our farms can be retained by a sufficient quantity of timber growth. In that respect, where we have cleared the timber away altogether, we have lost much in the fertility of our lands, particularly in dry seasons. I think we cannot show too great energy in the protection of the forest wealth we have and for the replacement of the wealth that is gone. I am in hopes that the use of aviation will in a measure assist in the work of protection from fire. It has been used also in the discovering of the pests that are destroying our forests. I am at a loss to know what results have been obtained in connection with the protection of our forests from these pests. Take even our shade trees; this season they are being attacked very severely by one of these pests, I do not know the name of it. I think that this province has done a good deal towards finding out some method of destroying this pest, but so far as I know, to date no genuine protection against its attacks has been provided.
There is a question now as to the export duty, or the prohibition of export. This is one of the difficulties that arises particularly in Ontario and Quebec. The settler goes into our forests in these provinces, and, unlike the settler going to the prairies, he has no land to plough until he clears a certain area. While he is doing that, working out a little home for himself, as our fathers did by clearing away the timber, his only means of living is by selling his pulp wood in the pulp wood areas. Now he objects very strongly to anything that tends to prevent him selling his pulp wood in the market that will give him the biggest price. I have been waited on by several of these men during recent months concerning this matter, and the contention of the settler is that if a prohibition or heavy export duty were imposed, he would be subject to a price dictated by the mill near his own home, and he believes or fears that the price he would receive for the pulp wood on the little clearing that he was preparing for agriculture, would be lessened to a degree that would be injurious. He might be protected in some way, but that is the objection raised in the two older provinces, as presented to me, not on behalf of the large exporter of pulp wood so much as the smaller settler who derives his living for two or three years from the sale of pulp wood while he is clearing his land. But something very radical will take place in this country before long in the protection of our forests, because it has been well pointed out that they are being denuded very rapidly and that in a few years our vast forest domain will be little more than a memory. I hardly know what to propose, because the government is studying the matter. I agree absolutely with everything that has been said with regard to the seriousness of the situation and the necessity of something being done, and I want to draw the attention of the committee to the objection that has been presented to the government concerning the small settler. Perhaps he could be protected in some way, but I cannot just now indicate how. If we in Canada are not going to look out for ourselves, our friends across the line are not going to do it for us. I may have wrong views, but my own opinion is that the Dominion of Canada, with its still vast expanse of timber area as well as other natural resources, ought to have a policy for the pepole of Canada, regardless of what other people do, treating them fairly, of course. But the further we go along in our national life the clearer it becomes to me that the nation that stands for itself at all times is the one that
341S
Supply-Interior

*will have the respect of all the other nations of the world, so long as it does it decently [DOT]and without reprisal to any other nation. I am strongly in favour of anything that will bring about better protection of our forests and lend encouragement to regrowing forests that have been denuded, as well as to tree-planting in those portions of the Dominion of Canada that are naturally without forest cover.
I hardly know what the minister means by a nation standing for itself. I think all the nations are doing that with a vengeance.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The right hon. leader of the Opposition spoke about reprisals. I feel as he does, and what I meant was that we should go along the line that we think that is best for the Dominion of Canada. The bugbear of reprisals is magnified in our minds, I think.
What about the big stick?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The big stick has never hurt us very much.
No, but we talk about having a stick.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I know, having something to dicker with. But if we dicker for our own interests first, we will be acting in accordance with my view of a nation's duty. With our resources in coal at both remote ends of this country, with our resources in timber, in fisheries, and above all our agricultural industry, we are in a position to stand erect, to do what we think is in the interest of the people of Canada, and to take chances on what any other nation wall do.

I should like to add a -word to this discussion. It was my lot to live for many years in a country that was right on the edge of just as dry a country as any place in Canada that I know of. I have had 'experience in raising timber in a dry country. Looking over the years that have passed, I know something about the effect in those countries of planting timber, and I want to say just a little regarding planting timber on the open prairie, in the West in particular. I agree with all that the ministerfMr. Graham) has said regarding the preservation of our timber.
I know that is needed. The country where I live, when I went in first, was practically all bush and timber, at least all that was not cultivated. Now, there is not much timber left in that country. I do not know how much influence this has had on the climate, and we do not know because the climate varies. We have cycles of dry years and

cycles of wet years; but it is my opinion that the clearing away of the timber has brought about more of a dry condition in our country. I know we have more wind in that country, because it is more open.
Coming back to the planting of timber in a prairie country, I think there should be some system, or an understanding of how to plant timber. I have an opportunity of knowing that by seeing what was done in the country where I lived so long. In the beginning the government had a policy to give a quarter section to any man who would plant forty acres of timber and take care of it. He was donated what we call a timber claim for S10, the same price as for taking a homestead. It was learned that enough people would not take up that land, plant forty acres in timber and attend to it, so as to get the results that the government wanted. Therefore the government cut this down, first to twenty acres and finally to ten acres. After they cut it down to ten acres, much more timber was planted in that country than was the case when they gave a man an opportunity of getting the land if he would plant forty acres of timber. That was more than they carei to take care of; it was a greater obligation than they wanted to assume in order to secure a quarter section. When they began to plant the ten acre lots in timber and to take care of them properly was when we began to see the best results. That timber had to be planted a certain distance apart; it had to be planted in a body. The idea was-and I believe it is a good one-that all timber planted should be planted in a body rather than in single rows, and I want to deal for just a moment with the question of planting in rows. I believe in a country where the wind is sweeping the soil and blowing it from one field to another and from one place to another, this can be stopped largely by planting rows of trees in different places. But when you plant one row of trees on one side of a farm, you cannot conserve very much moisture with that one row, because the vegetation there is not heavy enough, the leaves that fall will blow away, and you do not have on top of the ground an accumulation to conserve the moisture as you would have if the trees were planted in a body. The reason for planting timber in a body is to conserve the moisture, and after that the thing will take care of itself with the quantity of rainfall in any part of our western country. Provided timber is planted in a body and gets a start, the leaves falling and the vegetation there will accumulate a certain covering on top of the ground that will hold the moisture. In that way the trees will have better growth,

Supply-Interior
after cultivation is no longer needed, and, provided there is enough timber, the moisture will be conserved to go into the air and regulate the rainfall in that part of the country.
Some forty or fifty years ago in Nebraska, they commenced that kind of planting in a country just as dry as any part of Alberta, indeed as dry as any part of western Canada that 1 know of, and the rainfall in that country has been increased until we no longer hear of droughts whereas it was quite a common thing, and sometimes for several years at a time, to have drought in that country, thus preventing the normal growth of crops. That timber is holding enough moisture in the country to affect the climate to a considerable extent. I believe, as the minister said, when we remove the timber altogether, from any part of our country, we shall feel the result and the country will become drier. In the northern parts of China particularly that I have read about and st.udied more or less, they have floods, and they have droughts because their forests have been removed. Their land is rolling, and whenever rain occurs, the water rushes into the valleys and streams, goes away and does not he in the country so as to put moisture back into the air, conserve the moisture and ensure a normal rainfall.
Rows of trees may be all right; but as the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner) was speaking about the matter, this came into my mind. I knew well how they had to plant timber throughout that country under a system of getting enough trees to-[DOT]gether to hold sufficient moisture there to affect the rainfall. I believe, if in every quarter section in the western country, ten acres could be planted in timber, that would distribute the rainfall, and they would not have those periodical droughts from which they now suffer. I am satisfied of that from what I have read and from the experience I have had in a country similar to our own West.
I want to add just a word and to give the minister a little of the experience that I have had in growing timber. At first when we -went into that country, the people did not think very much of raising and cultivating timber. The prairies were burned regularly, and consequently the people had their difficulties from lack of rain. But after they had had their difficulties they began to want to get away from them, and they saw an opportunity to get out-in that way. They were led to take the government land as the government gave it to them and many of tthem after they had bought the land, planted
timber. I did that myself on a prairie farm and I know it is a pleasure; it is easy to raise timber if you know the right way to go about the work.
If the prairie grass were left untouched, in time it would form a very good covering or mulch. I have had occasion to study this problem and I know that in one particular county in which I lived in Nebraska the burning of the grass was rigidly prevented over a period of about ten years. At the end of that time there happened to be a drought, and experiment was made to ascertain the moisture of the land. Holes were dug to the depth of some ten feet where the land had been covered with the prairie grass during that ten years, and there was considerable moisture in that part; whereas on the other hand, wherever the grass had been burnt, the land remained quite dry, without any possibility of vegetation. So that there is no question, in my opinion at least, that it is possible to retain the moisture in the land if, whenever trees are cut down, others are planted to take their places. I have been much concerned in my part of the country to see the timber all cleared away. Every man seems to want to take an axe and cut down some tree, but he never thinks of planting another in its stead, and I believe that this practice is to be condemned.
We should have some sort of policy in Canada that would induce the people, if they are not willing to do it freely, to plant trees wherever they cut down timber. This is absolutely necessary for the preservation of our forests and for the purpose of ensuring moisture in the land. I know that in the part of the country from which I come, if you cut down timber and leave the land alone without burning you are bound to have a forest again. That has been my experience with land I have cleared if it was not broken at once. Whenever I have cut timber and left it for a few years, a thick growth of trees springs up. On the prairies, however, it is different; you must plant trees if you want to retain the plantation. I believe that if bonuses are advisable in any direction at all, there could be nothing in connection with which they would be more applicable and useful than in this particular matter.

There is no doubt about the importance of taking care of our forests which are being so rapidly destroyed not only by fire and insect pests, but by the lumber men and owners themselves. However, my object in rising just now is to ask the minister what proportion of this
Supply-Interior

money for fire prevention is distributed to the different provinces, and whether the province of Prince Edward Island receives anything under this vote? There was a time when the purpose was to cut down the forests as quickly as possible and get the trees out of the way. But that time has long passed, and the people are realizing now the fact that they have destroyed a very valuable asset. The time for undertaking the preservation of what is left of those forests has now arrived, and the people of my province feel that they should receive the same consideration in this matter as the western provinces. I would draw the attention of the government, whether the matter comes directly under this department or under the Department of Agriculutre, to the great destruction that is being caused by insect pests among the shade trees and orchards. I do not think this matter is receiving the attention it deserves. The shade trees are being attacked as well as the orchards, and I am afraid that they will be destroyed completely in the course of a very few years if some very effective methods are not adopted to cope with this menace. I might mention the havoc that has been played among our cherry trees in Prince Edward Island. These trees have been attacked not by the insects that are commonly known to the experts of the Department of Agriculture, but by some pest which has never been discovered, so that the cherry trees of the province have practically all died. Just as the tree blooms the leaves begin to wither, and the cause of this has never been investigated, so far as I know. This involves a serious loss to the province, for these trees are valuable. The minister might inform the committee in what proportion assistance is given to the various provinces for the prevention of fires, and whether anything is given to Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) raised a very difficult point of forest administration, namely, that the natural resources of the provinces are owned and administered by the provinces themselves with the exception of the three prairie provinces and the timber belt of British Columbia, which are Crown lands. The vote for fire purposes and indeed for all other purposes under this item is therefore confined to the area owned by the Crown; it does not apply to the provincial forest reserves, which are operated and taken care of by the provinces. So far as insect pests are concerned, however, this is a matter that comes under the Department of Agri-

culture and has received considerable attention at the hands of the Entomological branch, who have studied the problem altogether irrespective of the locality of any disease.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
For surveys and investigations of water and power resources and for administration of water powers, etc., $330,000.

Are there any departments
of government which undertake duties similar or related to the duties indicated in this vote? What is the attitude of the government with respect to the water-power privileges in the Banff National park?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Water
Powers Board is created by order in council and is given certain well-defined duties: it investigates the potentialities of the water-powers of Canada. I am not positive, but I think we have now made arrangements with every province in Canada in connection with this matter. Of course, the provinces that own their natural resources control their water-powers; but in order that we may have a comprehensive idea of the potentialities of the water-powers in Canada it is the work of this board to investigate, to measure, and in every other way to get accurate information as to where powers are located, what amount of power is available, and so forth. This work is being carried on throughout the whole Dominion. With regard to the second question of my hon. friend, nothing has been done. A good many representations have have been made, pro and con, we have heard a delegation from the power representatives, and the matter will be under consideration by the representatives of our own department on Tuesday next. No decision has yet been arrived at.

Is any other department of
the government concerned with the administration of water-powers, or does any other department .undertake work similar or related to the work of this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In administration? No.
Then I understand the situation to be that no other department of government is concerned with water-powers at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I would not go so far.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know to what extent my hon. friend means. The Department of Railways and Canals is to some extent interested in water-powers but not in an investigatory capacity.

Supply-Interior

The vote indicates that this department is interested not only in the surveying and investigation of the water and power resources of the Dominion but in the administration of water-powers as well. I want to know whether or not there are any other departments of government interested in any way in connection with water-powers; and, if so, what are the departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Department of Railways and Canals has authority,
I believe, to lease water-powers. But it is not concerned in measuring water-powers to the extent of controlling them for the purpose of leasing.
After a survey of a water-power has been made how is the information given to the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If any given water-power has been investigated the report is available to the public. That is the object of making the investigation, in order that it may become the property of the public.

I ask entirely as a matter of information. I notice that some large American firms are getting control of a number of water-powers in the West. We in the city of Winnipeg are faced with that situation at the present time in connection with our supply of water-power from the Winnipeg river. What procedure is taken to secure information in regard to new waterpower sites? Is advance information given to any individuals? What is the policy of the government in regard to leasing these powers? In short, how is it that one company can acquire a large number of water-power sites and so more or less control the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had better explain to my hon. friend that the provincial governments, where they are in possession of their natural resources, own the water-powers. Therefore the investigatory work on our part is merely to co-ordinate information for the whole of Canada, to get a comprehensive idea of the possibilities of water-power throughout the Dominion. We have not a word to say about who shall get control of the power. I think my hon. friend has in mind the situation of Ontario and Manitoba on the Winnipeg river?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We do not control the leasing of those powers. We have the information as to the power available and that sort of thing, which is of course very valuable, but the Ontario government
owns and controls the water-powers of the province. At least, the Ontario government maintains that it does own them. Perhaps I am going a step too far.
You are going far enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is disputed. However, subject to correction, that is the situation. There is an act on the statute books which is contrary to the contention of the Ontario government, for it describes these powers as being for the general advantage of Canada, which of course would bring them under the control of the Dominion government. Personally I have always assumed that the provinces do own their water-powers.

But in the case of those provinces that have not control over their natural resources the Dominion government becomes trustee, I suppose, of the water-powers. What is the policy of the government as to giving information concerning newly discovered water-powers?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are prepared to give the fullest information if we have investigated any particular water-power. Our work is not intended for the benefit of any private person, it is for the benefit of the public generally. Take, for example, in the province of Manitoba, we have investigated the -water-powers on the Nelson river and the Winnipeg river; this information is for the benefit of the public.

Coming down to administration, again as a matter of information, on what conditions can a company secure water-power rights? Does the government simply turn these powers over to the first applicant who can give assurance that he will develop them? Or does the government regard these powers as being essentially for the welfare of the whole people and administer them in a broad way for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think I can answer that question by simply saying "Yes." So far as I have come in contact with any application of this character-I do not recollect more than one-the applicants have had to demonstrate the purpose for which die power is to be used, the quantity of power required, and the period for -which it will be required, because the privilege is not granted to a private interest outright, it is merely leased for a definite period. That is the method by which control of these powers is maintained by the federal government. I do not know what method is pursued by the provincial governments.
Supply-Interior
Is the government prepared to take into consideration the development of water powers where they own the natural resources?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would entail the operation perhaps of a timber or manufacturing industry in the locality. However, there is another aspect that may loom up in the very near future, and that is the electrification of the railways, in which case undoubtedly, with our publicly-owned railway system, the government should be prepared, in my opinion, to retain the water-powers necessary and develop them for this electrification.

It was just with that thought in my mind that I made the suggestion to the minister, because it appears to me that if we are to have water powers available for electrification of the National Railway system, the time for the government to act is now, otherwise they will find all the available water powers under the control of private ownership.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am speaking now strictly of federally controlled power, because after all it will be small in amount in comparison with the total power required for the electrification of our railways throughout the Dominion, as it is only in the three prairie provinces that we have control of the natural resources. No water powers will be leased there except for a definite purpose; that is, we are not going to simply lease water powers to private individuals to enable them to get control.
But have we not already specific instances of that very thing being done?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There may have been in the past; I am speaking for the immediate future and for last year. I would insist that any lease should be contingent upon the supply of power being utilized for the purpose for which it was leased. I do not think we should decline to lease power to any private individual for legitimate development, but on the other hand, I do say that no more power should be leased to the individual than he actually requires for the purpose intended, and that on no account should control pass out of the Dominion.

I simply wish to utter a note of warning to the government in this matter. We anticipate within a few years that electrical power will have developed even to the extent of running some of our railways, and if the government does 
not at once take steps to safeguard these power sites they will find when they require them that they are all in the hands of private owners, who will hold up the government in a manner similar to that of which we have had examples in the past.
What is the term of years for which these leases of power sites are granted? Is there a specified term, or is it an indeterminate lease?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Regard is had to the use to which the power will be put and the probable duration of the power requirements. In addition, there is provision for the taking back of the power at actual cost at any time. A man may require power for development in connection with his manufacturing concern for, say, twenty-five years. Or take the case that I suppose the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), is ppeaking about, power development for Winnipeg-that undoubtedly will be required for all time to come. I am thinking more particularly of mills and establishments of that character; the provision to which I have referred is inserted in all such leases.

Out in western Canada practically every lease that is issued is transferable. Now, this is a very important point. Does the minister not think the time has arrived when all leases whether grazing leases, coal, timber or power leases, should be made non-transferable so that those who desire to come in and devlop these natural resources will not be held up by speculators for large sums of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: With very few exceptions, all classes of leases are made non-tran-ferablc; that is, they cannot be transferred without the consent of the minister. In other words, the transfer cannot be a transaction between two private persons, one holding the lease and the other desirous of getting it.
Does that apply to a situation where a lease has not been developed, or is the minister's consent given only where there has been development?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It applies to every lease. It is a provision of the lease itself.

I want to enter a protest against the granting of leases in cases where those who received the lease in the first place have done no development work at all, but are simply holding the lease up for the purposes of speculation. I would not have

Supply-Interior
so much objection in cases where there had been development and there was a desire to transfer the lease, but where no development has taken place I maintain that it is a wrong principle to permit the transfer. It is my belief that one of the real reasons why our country has not developed as it should have is because the speculative element have got leases for our natural resources and are holding them up so that those who desire to use those natural resources will have to pay large sums of money for them. I would ask the minister to allow this item to stand until after we come here to-night, because the matter is a very important one.
At six o'clock, the Speaker resumed the chair and the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
