speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
For surveys and investigations of water and power resources and for administration of water-powers, etc., $330,000.

When we rose at six
o'clock we were discussing the possibilities of leasing the water-powers in the three prairie provinces. I should like to bring before the House some information with regard to the manner in which leases, not particularly water leases, but other leases, have operated in this country. First, I say that it is necessary to put into force such regulations as will conserve these water-powers in western Canada for the use of the people, so that we can utilize them. No doubt we hope in the near future that western Canada will develop more rapidly than in the past, and, because of the fact that our water-powers' in that country are strictly limited, it should be necessary to see to it that they are conserved for the use of the people.
I will cite one or two examples of what I mean by conserving the water-powers of Canada, and I am going to present some examples which have occurred recently. About two years' ago there were supposed to be m the Fort Norman field large quantities of oil, and people made a rush to that particular portion of the Northwest Territories for the purpose of taking out oil claims in the distiict. I will tell the House how it worked out in the long run. I will give one example of a man who lived in Edmonton, and perhaps the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) is well acquainted with this case. This man went to Fort Norman, and I believe it took him about two months to go there and return, at a cost of less than $5,000. He staked out his claim at Fort Norman, came back to Edmonton, registered the claim, and a few days after he had registered it he sold it for $310,000, making a profit of $305,000 for approximately two months' work. The position we take is that that man contributed nothing to the well-being of this country. By using the form of lease that we have at the present time he was enabled to make a large sum of money without contributing one iota to the welfare of Canada. We maintain that those conditions of leasing are not in the best interests of Canada.
This statement is applicable also to our water powers. At the present time there is an oil development in southern Alberta. When I was in Calgary a few days prior to coming to Ottawa for the session, I noticed .in the streets placards advertising oil leases for sale. Hon. members can well understand that those oil leases were offered for sale by men who were speculating in them, and the House will also understand that an operator must pay the price that these speculators demand before he can start operations with these oil leases. That, Mr. Chairman, is not in the best interests
Supply-Interior

of Canada, and I believe one of the reasons why Canada has not developed as she should have developed is the fact that we have allowed speculators to monopolize our natural resources to the detriment of the country.
I will give the House another example of something that happened in Alberta. Hon. members will remember that Saskatchewan and Alberta came into the confederation in the year 1905. Parliament at that time thought it advisable to retain the natural resources, not only of these two provinces but also of Manitoba. The federal authority, of course, had to deal with these natural resources. Since 1305, in the province of Alberta, over 800 coal fields have been opened up. Coal leases have been sold by speculators ever since the time that coal leases were available. Coal mines have been opened up to such an extent that five times more coal is mined in Alberta than we can profitably utilize under present conditions. About the year 1913 the Canadian Northern completed its branch line from Saskatoon to Calgary, and the line runs through the Drumheller coal fields. On the first coal that we received from Drumheller we had to pay the construction rate, which was a higher rate than we are paying at the present time. At that particular time we could buy screened coal, for from $4.75 to $5.25 per ton. To-day we cannot buy that coal under $7.75. For what reason? Simply because we have in Alberta five times more coal mines opened up than we actually need. There is, I am told, $50,000,000 invested in coal properties in Alberta alone, and, for the small amount required for western Canada, it means that they have to charge a high price for the coal, in order to take care of the overhead that they have invested in these coal mines. I think it would be good policy if the department over which my hon. friend has control at the present time should take cognizance of conditions, and say whether it is necessary to give leases, for instance, for coal mines, and so forth in Alberta. What is the use of allowing people to put good money into properties that will not be a paying proposition, unless they are in a position to charge more for their product than it is actually worth?
I should like to bring another matter to the attention of the Minister of the Interior. He will remember that in the year 1909 the southern part of Alberta was opened up for settlement. Up to that time this portion to the south had always been reserved, for some reason or other, but the department decided to open up this particular part of southern Alberta. They sent literature to the United States, sent it all over Canada, and to Great
fMr. Gardiner.]
Britain, for the purpose of inducing people to come to that particular section of the country; they advertised that the land was good, that they would have free homesteads, and stated also that you could buy a quarter section of land which was known as the preemption, for $3 an acre. We have had hard conditions there, but the people in that district at the present time believe they could make a success of their enterprise if they had some of the rough land that is around there for community grazing purposes. The minister will remember the Alberta members interviewing him more than once last year for the purpose of trying to get some of these areas opened up for community grazing leases. At the time I was in Calgary prior to coming down for the session I saw advertised in many of the windows in places where they were selling land that grazing leases were for sale. For instance, I might give you a particular case.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should like to draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that the question of grazing leases can hardly be debated under the item of water and power resources.

I submit to your ruling, but I am leading up to the question, inasmuch as I desire to draw to the attention of the minister the effects of past policy in respect to the manner in which leases have been granted. That applies to water-power leases as well as to grazing leases. I cite these cases merely for the purpose of giving the minister an outline of the situation. When I was in Calgary prior to coming down to this session of parliament, I saw grazing leases there for sale, and if I remember well, there were five thousand acres of leased grazing land. The price that the leased land was offered at was $1.10 an acre. Those who had this particular leased land had a lease on it only for grazing purposes; but because of our system of leases, these get into the hands of speculators and become a speculative proposition, instead of one for the development of Canada. I trust that, with the few examples I have given to the minister, he will try to evolve some different system, wherebv all leases, including water-power leases, shall be issued only to those who are going to use them, and they shall not be made transferable until such time as they have been fairly well developed.

The minister gave it as his opinion that we should continue to regard water-powers as belonging to the various provinces. I am quite aware of the fact that such

Supply-Interior
has been the general idea in the past. I do not know how the matter stands from a strictly legal point, even according to the old conception; but I should like to suggest that with the developments which have gone on in connection with the use of electrical power, the time has come when we shall have to alter our opinions in this regard. We have been told that the air is free, and yet within very recent years, with the development of aerial navigation, the whole idea has been absolutely changed, and to-day we have certain conventions with regard to aerial navigation. We also have some very definite regulations with regard to the transmission of messages through the air. That just illustrates the changes that are taking place because of changed conditions brought about by these newer inventions. I submit that recent developments in the electrical world have made necessary some change with regard to our ideas in connection with these water-powers.
I do not desire to-night to anticipate to any extent the debate which is likely to take place with regard to the Lake of the Woods, a bill concerning which is now before the House, but I should like to refer to that very briefly just as illustrating this point and the necessity of altering our policy. I think we all recognize to-day that the question of the electrification of railways must come before us in a practical form in the not distant future. Anyone who knows the northern stretches of Canada must realize the immense possibilities of electrifying our railways without any very serious trouble, if we have control of the water-powers that exist almost from coast to coast across Canada. The fact that we have already as a part of the national property, a great railway system, makes it essential that we look a little bit ahead in this matter. We were told the other day in this House that the children of darkness are wiser in their day and generation than the children of light. It would seem as if some of the private exploiters in this country are a great deal wiser than those who are charged with the administration of our public affairs. Perhaps very naturally we are proceeding on the old idea of local administration and private exploitation of these resources. But when we consider that if we are going to electrify our system, that would have to be done, not by the possession of this, that and the other water-power, but by the possession and exploitation of water-powers over a distance of three thousand miles, then we begin to understand the necessity of taking a different line of action from that which we have taken in the past.
In passing, I should like to call attention to another development which must take
place in the near future, and that is the use of electricity for heating purposes. I was reading only the other day an article dealing with the report of the American government with regard to super-stations. According to that report, it will be feasible in the not distant future to supply great central stations which will provide for the heating of many of our cities. We are considering doing this in my own city of Winnipeg as supplementary to the coal supply. These things are matters that are not simply in the realm of the ideal or speculative; they are rapidly becoming matters of urgent public importance.
I would urge upon the minister that in making these surveys, he do so, not with the thought of securing information that would be available merely for local enterprises, but rather having in view the development of the whole of our electrical power as one great system. The minister a little while ago suggested that he was afraid that if we began to operate some of these water powers, we might have to go into certain industries, [DOT]such as the pulp or the lumber industry. I do not know that that is essential, at least not in the immediate future, because we could do as is done in other places, sell this power to those who are going into these industries. That might be an immediate solution; but I would emphasize that we should regard the whole undertaking as one great system. For instance, the Lake of the Woods is fed by a series of streams, having many water powers, and the Lake of the Woods in turn feeds the Winnipeg river which is the source of our power for the city of Winnipeg. On the other hand, there is tributary to the Winnipeg river the English river which is fed by other lakes, sepecially Lac Seul. All these bodies and streams of water, some in Ontario, some in Manitoba and some along the boundary line between Ontario and the United States, form naturally one unified system, and it is impossible to deal with one particular waterfall. If one attempts to exploit one waterfall, there is great danger that other waterfalls may be interfered with. If one raises the levels on certain lakes, as we all know, that may have a veiy serious effect hundreds of miles away. This has happened in this particular instance and raised questions of international importance, and we have had our International Joint. Commission dealing with the problem. The particular dispute that is to come before this House is an interprovincial proposition. I am not going to go into that matter to-night. To me it is a minor matter as to which province controls the situation. The fact is that neither can adequately develop the water powers without
Supply-Interior

having regard to the rights of the other, and the system should be regarded as a unit. Let me offer one particular illustration of how seriously dealing with one part may affect another. In 1922, the town of Sioux Lookout was promised a lease by the Ontario government of the Pelican rapids power site on Lac Seul. This power site is so situated that it can only be of commercial value provided that the water level on Lac Seul is maintained at its normal height, hence t)ie raising of the lake level for regulations and storage purposes destroys Pelican rapids as a power site. The promise of this lease was immediately recognized by Manitoba as a serious menace to the scheme of regulation recommended for adoption, as it sacrificed the development of 160,000 horse power on the English and Winnipeg rivers for a possible 3,000 horse power at Pelican rapids. A net loss of 157,000 horse power to the two provinces.
This illustrates the situation all over the country, and is a matter of urgent public importance, so I suggest that in the making of these surveys we should not regard the problem merely as one of providing for particular private enterprises, but rather should draft a general scheme for the exploitation of water-powers, with their wonderful electrical energy, for the benefit of all the people.

I want to ask three or four questions touching this matter, but first of all I want the minister to answer this query: What concessions in the way of water-power have been granted to the adjoining republic by this government in northern Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There was me on the Saskatchewan river, but it has been cancelled. There was also one on the Nelson river over which there has been considerable controversy, and it too has lapsed. At the moment, therefore, there are really no concessions extant in the north of Manitoba. I might say to my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner) with respect to the question of grazing leases, that these leases cannot be transferred except with the consent of the minister. Upon the expiry of a lease we notify the provincial government, who undertake the work of community grazing; and this is done in Alberta and Saskatchewan. In Saskatchewan there is a ranch being utilized for this purpose. If the provincial government desires land for community grazing, then the lease is held for that purpose.

I understand that this is not the case. I have had interviews with the officers of the department who inform 
me that the Justice department interpreted one of the sections of the regulations - to give preference to the owner to renew the lease within four years of its expiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is true; that applies to the owners. But we have an arrangement with the Alberta goverjnment whereby, when a lease expires, we transfer it to the provincial government for community grazing, unless the lessee renews the lease; and this is not very often done. It is news to me to learn that there has been trafficking in grazing leases. I was not aware of the fact, but I take my hon. friend's word for it. Evidently someone must have been endeavouring to dispose of leases in that way. With respect to water-powers, practically 80 per cent of what is stated to be desirable has already been done. The controversy between Manitoba and Ontario is a considerable one and will come up for discussion, no doubt, when the bill proposed by the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) is under consideration. I am not going to touch that question to-night, because I shall probably have something to say about it later on. But that is one of the difficulties we have to contend with.

In view of the answer given by the minister with regard to water-power concessions cancelled in northern Manitoba, is there any concession granted by this government in Ontario near the boundary of Manitoba? I was talking with a friend a year and a-half ago and he told me there had just been granted a very valuable concession in the way of water-power and pulp wood in northern Manitoba, as I understood. It might have been- in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The officer informs me that there are none except at Great Falls on the Winnipeg river, to the Manitoba Power Company.
Is that the one?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that is the closest one to the Ontario boundary.
Is that the company whose territory was extended and over which there was a discussion in the House on a former occasion?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. My hon. friend asked me what concession had been granted close to the Ontario boundary. That is the closest one to the boundary.

What is the meaning of "investigations of water and power

Supply-Interior
resources"? Does that include underground water such as well water?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that is under the supervision of Mr. Dowling of the Geological branch.
Has the minister's department any jurisdiction over the water-powers in Ontario and Quebec? Do I understand that all this money is spent in Alberta and Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; I explained that this afternoon. We are making an investigation, measuring the possibilities in every province, and we have an agreement with the provinces to facilitate this work. We do not control the water-powers; we simply investigate and find out the possibilities of water-power throughout Canada as a whole.
Is this government reimbursed by the provinces for that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
For the investigation of the fuel and power resources of the Dominion and for the expenses of the Dominion Power Board, $10,000.
I thought we had a vote for this board the other day under another item.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is special work that was started before my time. It consists in an investigation of the St. Lawrence river which is carried out by two engineers of the department, Mr. H. A. Mat-thewson. and Mr. A. B. Lamb, who are engaged in a study of the St. Lawrence river power and navigation project. The expenses of the investigation are charged up to this item.
Have they anything to do with fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know why fuel should have been included in the item; I have been asking that question myself.
Mr. Chairman, did the minister explain the word "fuel"?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was asking why that word came in. It should not be there. Mr. Challies himself is on the Fuel Investigation Board for which we passed a vote in the Mines branch. The word "fuel" should be eliminated. This is purely an investigation of the St. Lawrence canal scheme with respect to the power possibilities in the event of the scheme being undertaken.

Why not
put that item under the preceding one? It covers very much the same work.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is correct about that, but evidently this is the way the item was started and it has not been changed. If it was to be continued, I agree with him it should all go in the one item.
Has the power board made any investigation of the possible water-power which might be developed in the Highwood river?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The officers are not sure that they made a thorough investigation of the Highwood river, but they suggest the power would be very small judging by the flow-although I see by to-night's paper they are having a considerable flow there these days.

Has any report been
made by the Dominion Power Board on the St. Lawrence power possibilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. A report was made by the International Joint Commission, and in discussing this with Mr. Challies he mentioned that a careful investigation might disclose several inaccuracies in that report, although he was not reflecting upon the report itself. Indeed, that is one of the difficulties we have to contend with, that we have not any definite knowledge of the possibilities of the scheme.

I presume this is to check up the report of the International Joint Commission. In this connection, I hope the government will study the project seriously, because it is of very great importance to the province of Ontario that exactly what is possible there in water-power development should be known.

My memory is that this vote was started largely for the purpose of getting data so that Canada's representatives would have something definite to go on in connection with the St. Lawrence scheme when they appeared before the International Joint Commission. I think the vote was a good deal larger formerly.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My recollection is that it was the same.
Supply-Interior
It was a larger vote for the purpose of securing data to be used for that inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The vote
covered the work of the board generally. Is it the power board my hon. friend is speaking about, or the direct investigation of the St. Lawrence possibilities?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Two men are engaged on that work this year.
What are they doing now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When the matter was introduced last year by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) I discussed it with Mr. Challies, and I learned then that we had two men engaged on this work continuously checking the report of the engineers of the International Joint Commission, investigating the backflow that appears to be in evidence here, particularly at what would be the mouth of the canal, and the power possibilities for the purpose my hon. friend has pointed out.
Can we look forward to an interim report? Because I should like to get the data as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, we
could get a report of the situation as it is up-to-date.

In the near
future?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

How long is it going to take to check this up? These men have been at it now for a year. Surely the work ought to be done by now. Is it a continuous job so that these men may be kept on whether there is anything to be done or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I would not say that. It is difficult for a layman to state how much has been accomplished by these men. My hon. friend will agree, however, that accurate information should be had in connection with this project and the power possibilities, because it is a tremendously big undertaking and some day undoubtedly Canada will have to come to a decision about it. I shall be glad to get an interim report in respect to what they have discovered up to date. It should not take more than this year to thoroughly check up the whole thing.

I quite agree with the minister that it is very important for us to get

accurate information, but I would be somewhat critical of a couple of engineers who have been working at this so long and as yet have made no report. I do not pose as a technical man, but it seems to me two years ought to be sufficient to check up a report of that kind.
I understand the report of the International Joint Commission dealt only with the water-power on the part of the St. Lawrence which flows between Canada and the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend's information is at fault; the report included both the Canadian and American.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
For surveys and inspections in connection with the administration of the Irrigation Act, etc., $200,000.
What irrigation project is this?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No new
work in irrigation surveys was undertaken; they are practically completed with the exception of the centre Alberta irrigation scheme, which embraces the area north of the Red Deer river through the constituency of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner) and the Bow river valley. I concluded, however, that the surveys had gone to that point where we could get an indication of the probable cost of the project and that it would not be necessary to continue the lateral surveys. Our vote this year is to pay for the completion of the various projects and meet the cost of the staff in Calgary. We spend $54,945 in Calgary, for the permanent staff and $40,335 for the field staff. The permanent staff at Ottawa, which takes care of both reclamation and irrigation, takes $10,470 and the field surveys and experimental and demonstration work, $88,060. Then, there are the travelling expenses of officers of the staff, amounting to $11,510; equipment at Calgary, instruments, camp equipment, transport, and so on which are required yearly, $4,280; expenses of office at Ottawa, $10,400, total, $200,000 this year for both services.

Do I understand from
the minister that the federal government makes the surveys in all these various projects that are under way in Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, they
made all the original surveys.

What is meant by the words in the item, "administration of the Irrigation act"?

Supply-In terior

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is for field inspection, surveys, etc. There has been some demonstration work; at Brooks in southern Alberta we have a farm on which demonstration work has been carried on, to indicate proper methods of putting the water on the land and generally how best to run an irrigated farm.

Is that a Dominion
government farm?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I understood they were
called experimental farms. I notice you refer to them as demonstration farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is an
experimental station, but it is under the control of the Irrigation branch for irrigation purposes alone.

I hope no one will question for a minute this item of expenditure; it is one of the most important items that appears in this whole list. It is an attempt by the Dominion government to accomplish work in southern Alberta that should
9 p.m. have been accomplished before settlers were ever admitted there. When we came into that southern Alberta country in the early years it seemed to us that we had everything that nature could give us to make it a successful farming district. We had as rich soil as could be found anywhere on earth. The settlers who came in there had the necessary capital with which to go to work, and they had implements and equipment. They had intelligence; they had the industry, and they had above all else the glorious sunshine of that country. The people in the northern part of the province apparently do not have as much of the sunshine that we glory in. All these things combined, however, were of little effect, we found as the years went on, without water. Water was king, but an absent king in that southern country.
Now the government has been aiding us to the limited extent of providing for the necessary general and preliminary survey work to determine the quantity and source of our water supply and to lay out the systems which would help us to bring that water on to the land so that we would have all the elements necessary for a permanent and profitable agriculture. That has been the whole purpose of the government work, and the amount expended to that end is not a drop in the bucket when you think of the importance of placing agriculture in that country on a firm and dependable foundation.
Let me illustrate that: Take one of our wet years-for we have wet years in that country. The district that was covered by a survey board that went over that country in 1921, known as the drought area-that district in 1915 shipped out 41,000,000 bushels of grain. That was a wet year. In the following year, 1916, 37,000,000 bushels were shipped out; the drought period had begun to come on. In the next year, 1917, there was comparatively little moisture in the soil and our shipments dropped to 18,000,000 bushels. The drought continued; in 1918 our shipments dropped to 5,000,000 bushels1, and in 1919 to 4,000,000. Not only was the output of our grain affected to that marked extent, but at the same time the forage of that country became depleted; there was no feed for the stock, so that there waS a heavy loss in all the branches of stock raising as well as in our grain production. These losses have involved also the loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars to the Dominion of Canada, to its railways, to its banks, to all the various commercial factors connected with the business of farming.
The work covered by this vote was an attempt on the part of the Dominion government to help us correct these difficulties due to lack of moisture. We have gone ahead with this minimum of assistance and have developed large irrigation areas. In the first place we had to start with the old A. R. and I, area, comprising about 130,000 acres, and later we developed the Taber area, comprising 17,000 acres.
We have just recently completed the Lethbridge northern irrigation district of 105,000 acres. We have laid out besides a district running south of Macleod and embracing 60,000 acres. We have completed the United Irrigation project of 23,000 acres west of Cards-ton. All over that country people are at work endeavouring to overcome the difficulties which nature has placed in their way from lack of water or moisture, and this is but a minimum of expenditure on the part of the government in helping us to overcome those difficulties. I hardly believe that a word is necessary from anybody in this House to sanction this expenditure on the part of the federal government. It is not only essential to the welfare of the farmers there, but it is necessary to the upkeep of your transportation agencies, necessary for the success of the merchant, of the banks, and of all business interests throughout that district. Had I known this item was coming up this evening I think I would have talked to you for about an hour and a half or two hours as some of our friends do on this side, but

Supply-Interior

it is so apparent that this expense is entirely wise on the part of the federal government that I scarcely feel it is necessary to add another word.

I do not wish to criticize the vote at all in view of what my colleague from Lethbridge says but as I understand it these surveys always precede the work. The minister said there are no new projects contemplated or under way. Why is it that surveys'need to go on after the work on the undertaking has started?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When I say that no new work is contemplated or no new works are to be started it does not mean that the works that are being examined are completed. There is completion work to be done on one or two of them. As a matter of fact, I do not know any area in the province of Alberta at the moment that is not surveyed-that is where it would be possible to irrigate. We are simply completing the work that has been undertaken.
What is the situation with regard to the irrigation project known as the William Pearce, or the Northern' Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I spoke of it a moment ago. However, I will tell my hon. friend that we have a report on that project which would indicate that it is feasible. It will cost in the neighbourhood of $50,000,000 and embraces a considerable area of the province of Saskatchewan north of the Red Deer river. There is still a considerable amount of preliminary survey work to be done. For example none of the laterals have been surveyed, just the main ditch and proving the feasibility of the scheme. In view of the fact that it will involve such a huge expenditure I thought it was premature to expend money on survey work until there was some likelihood of the scheme being gone on with.
Do I understand the survey work on that project has ceased?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Except to the extent of proving the scheme feasible and its probable cost.
There is no more surveying going on there then?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: None this year.
What is the amount that will be spent in the province of Alberta under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is practically all spent there. I gave the items a moment ago. They will be in Hansard.

This is almost entirely an Alberta project, in fact it was started, as I recollect, some years ago, I forget the exact year, for the purpose of showing the province, what could be done, where the money could be spent to the best advantage, and how these arid lands could be made fertile? The idea always was that we should be in advance of the work of the province. I wanted to find out from my hon. friend whether we are still properly in advance of the province's work?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I do not know of any other project except a small scheme that might be undertaken by private individuals for their own particular benefit as to which we have also been giving advice. In such a case as that it is not a very costly process. One man can take the levels and ascertain whether or not a private individual, or three or four individuals, could have a small scheme of their own. Outside of that the province is well covered.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Reclamation of Dominion lands by drainage, (including revote of $36,000), $129,000.

What is the policy of the department with regard to the reclaiming of these lands? In my own constituency there is quite a number of reclamation projects that have been surveyed. Some have been handed over apparently to private individuals with the understanding that they reclaim the land, while others have simply been surveyed and nothing done. Is it the minister's intention to have these lands reclaimed by the government, for instance the one at Lesser Slave lake, or simply adopt a waiting attitude for the present?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Slave river project, I think, is what my hon. friend has reference to.
That is one of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Slave river is navigable and comes under the jurisdiction of the Public Works department. I cannot give my hon. friend information as to what can be done, although I know that application has been made to the department for surveys to determine the probable cost of straightening the river and lowering the level of the lake.

Supply-Interior
There is another at High Prairie west of Dewar. Then there is also one south of Entwistle.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
High
Prairie? That is off Slave lake.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There were surveys made by our department there last year.
What is the intention in regard to those lands? They cannot be homesteaded. Is it intended to reclaim the lands and then sell them?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I might say I have gone over this several times. I do not know ,what the attitude of the department was in the past with respect to this work but this is our present attitude: We will do the initial survey work and prove the scheme. We are glad to undertake that responsibility and expense just as we do in irrigation work, but when it comes to the actual carrying out of the scheme either the municipality or the province, preferably the province, would have to undertake the supervision of the work because they are close to the scene and will know the value of the work much better than the Dominion government would. There is a good deal to be said about draining areas that are Crown lands prior to settlement. Most of these lands, with the exception of some projects that are under way, such as the Carrot river scheme, are a considerable distance from railway facilities. The sending of people into these new areas where there are no railway facilities does not appear to be good business, when we have such a large amount of land lying within reasonable distance of a railway. If the province cares to undertake projects of that sort we have an arrangement with both Saskatchewan and Alberta to turn the Crown lands that may be involved in any of these schemes over to them, the lands to be sold on a basis similar to the provisions that govern the sale of school lands at a fixed price per acre.
How much was spent last year?

I want to say a word in regard to the matter the minister touched on. It seems to me many of our difficulties particularly the railway difficulty have been brought about by spreading our settlement over too large a territory. A group of people have been encouraged to go into a district, perhaps good enough in itself but far removed from railway facilities, and of course, in a
219 J
short time they are asking for railways. I was glad to hear him say that it did not look like good business to encourage people to settle in districts far removed from railways. I think the department should incline to the policy of consolidating our settlement, rather than spreading it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In answer to the question of the hon. member for West York, the amount spent last year was $170,000. I may say we are cutting down this work and we will not require that much this year.
What did we get for that money last year? Where is the work going on?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There was work at Waterhen lake in Saskatchewan and in the Carrot river district in Manitoba. Those two projects referred to are still incomplete.

Would the minister say what progress has been made in regard to reclaiming what has been termed the Kootenay flats in the Creston district? It is an international question, I believe. There is an area of 70,000 acres that ought to be reclaimed. What progress has been made in the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have not done anything on any of these projects. Would it be the work of the provincial government the hon. member refers to? They have the Sumas lake project, and they have the project at Chilliwack.

This project is located in the eastern part of British Columbia, bordering on the state of Idaho. It is an area of 70,000 acres. Half of it is in British Columbia and half in Idaho. There has been a good deal of correspondence in the last ten years, I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would be in the territory controlled by British Columbia. All the area we would be operating in would be the block on each side of the railway.

I believe it has developed into an international question, and the negotiations would have to be carried out by the federal government. Certain negotiations have been in progress for years between the Canadian and United States governments, and, if possible, I would like to find out what progress was made along that line last year. Up to a year ago, I had a copy of the return of the progress made in previous years and I believe it was left to the federal government to carry on the negotiation with
Supply-Interior

the United States government, but, as far as the work that has been done is concerned, it has been between the province of British Columbia and the state of Idaho. I believe they are being held back awaiting certain negotiations to be carried out by the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This particular branch of the government's service knows nothing about it. I will get any information we may have with respect to any negotiation between our government and the government of the United States.

I realize that this matter probably does not come directly under this vote, but I was at a loss to know under what vote it did come. I do not think it is under Dominion Lands although the Dominion government has certain jurisdiction.
Are there any reclamation nrojects where there is a contract with private ndividuals, or is the department carrying jut all these projects in the way the minister suggested a little while ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not atch the question. Did the hon. member ask f we were making contracts?
Yes. I asked if there were any contracts?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, in
Saskatchewan.
None in Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Canadian national parks and historic sites, $1,250,980.

I would like to have something definite from the minister as to whether the department is prepared to have an independent board of managers control, for public purposes, lands which are not used for historic sites but on which historic sites have been erected. Would the minister consider the use of lands given for historic sites as playgrounds, so long as there was no interference with the particular portion used for the historic site? I want something definite on that, right away, on behalf of my town.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon.
member will get his municipality to make an application we will be very glad to give hem for the use free of charge this particular area or any land we are not utilizing for the definite purpose of placing memorials and whatever may be necessary in connection with those memorials.

With all due deference, I do not think the municipalities are particularly concerned. We are a public body of citizens making application, the best citizens of the community. Will the minister put these sites in the hands of a committee who will safeguard the matter, under a lease from the minister, on proper terms to be set forth by the minister? In my constituency we have four or five municipalities, East Hants, West Hants, Hantsport and other places seeking incorporation. In cases where there are twenty-eight or twenty-nine acres of land, where an acre or two would embrace all the historic sites, we ask that the public citizens of the town be entitled to have a committee appointed to manage the remaining lands in the interests of children and to provide playgrounds. The site in my town is the best sliding ground for children in the winter time, and in summer it is a fine place for children to play. I do not think any official of the department should have the right to say to the young children who are playing there "Get off the ground" or "Do this" or "Do that", because this is an historic site, and I want to get a direct understanding from the minister that when we make an application to him we will have a right to use the lands that are not absolutely necessary for the historic sites, not leased because we are not prepared to pay anything for them. A poor man like myself could not pay any money for them.
What I want is that the children shall have the right to use this land as a play ground, for a toboggan slide in the winter time, as a place in the summer to put their tents, and in every way for them to be accorded the proper rights for youngsters who want to get out and play. We may all be men, and we are apt, when we ask for things, to stick too much to technical rules. I do not want to recite the old poem of "The Children" and that sort of thing; but on behalf of the citizens of that town, I want to apply to the Minister of the Interior, under whose administration this matter comes, to have the land which is not used specifically for the site allocated under a proper committee for play grounds for the children. I want a definite answer.
Will the minister inform the committee as to how much of this appropriation is for marking historical sites?

If my hon. friend will
permit me, I should like to have a definite answer from the minister. I do not want to go to the department when parliament has prorogued and to be told that this is the rule,

Supply-Interior
the law; that the other regulation has to be abided by. We are prepared to accept every reasonable regulation, but what we want is something definite. If my hon. friend thinks he is going to put me aside in that way, he is far astray. I want to see fair play for the children. I have youngsters of my own, and I want to see the children of to-day in my town get what I will demand for my youngsters one or two years hence. I want play grounds for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Let me say
for the information of my hon. friend, that many of the speeches that have been made in this House this evening have been pointed directly at the preservation of these very grounds, the preservation of the property of the Crown for the purposes of the Crown. I have no particular objection to the hon. gentleman or his friends; I think they would be perfectly reliable and responsible. That is not the suggestion at all. But in the past it has come to my notice that grounds of this character, that ought of necessity to be preserved for the public interest, have been secured by private people who have then proceeded to exploit the public. Therefore, there is only one safe course for the department to pursue, and that is to have the municipality behind any application of this sort. Then one knows that the public interest will be preserved in connection with matters of this kind.

With all due deference
to the opinion of the minister, there may be a divergence of opinion. Sometimes in small towns there are members of council who have no children or whose families are grown up, and who have absolutely no sympathy with children on that account. We find that in connection with school boards. The men on them are mature; their families are grown up, and they have no regard for the fellow with a young family growing up. I do not think the minister should impose any condition as regards municipalities stating what should or should not be done. As long as the minister is satisfied that the proper portion necessary for historical purposes is conserved, where it is shown by responsible citizens that they are prepared to see that the balance is set aside for playgrounds, that should be done. Nobody is going to exploit the public in a small place like mine; but municipal councils move slowly; often they are actuated by politics, and the children suffer. There are twenty-eight or twenty-nine acres on this site in the town of Windsor. I do not want any municipality or anybody else to control it; I want to go to the minister and to be
able to say to him:	Here is a place, old
Fort Edward in Windsor; you can fence up a couple of acres on which the old block house and other places stood; but let the children have the balance for toboggan slides to play in the winter. We do not call them toboggan slides in country places. It is only in Ottawa where the ministers of the Crown reside that they are called toboggan slides. We in the country places call them ordinary slides; that is all. Then, in the summer time let us have some place where the children can put their tents. I will guarantee to the minister that there will be no politics in the matter; that only the children will be provided for. If the minister will ask me to-day, 1 will give him the names of three people in my town, two of whom are opponents, one an active opponent of mine, and others who will manage this place because they have children the same as I have. Men with families which are grown up have no right to deny to a man who has youngsters, or who expects one day to enjoy looking at his youngsters around him, the right of having a playground for his children, nor to tie up the matter with a great deal of red tape. If there is anything of that sort, I am going to oppose this item. No municipal, control for me.
I should like to know how much of this appropriation is for the marking of historic sites, and what historic sites the government propose to mark this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Twenty-five thousand dollars.
Before I conclude, I want an answer. If the children are not entitled to be represented here, I am their representative.
Can the minister inform the committee as to how far advanced the work is on the cairn which is being erected at Port Dover to mark the wintering site of Fathers Dollier and Galinee?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The contract for the cairn is let at Port Dover at a cost of $600, including a wharf, I believe.

May I ask the minister what I am to expect? I want for Fort Edward, in the town of Windsor, apart from the site which is absolutely necessary for public purposes, a park to be placed under the direction of a proper committee for the use of the children. I am not going to w'aive that issue, and I want a direct answ'er. I am not asking that the whole thing be set aside for a few people to get together, say in the city of Hali-

Supply-Interior
fax or any other place, to recite fancy papers about what Sir John So-and-So said years and years ago. That is all very fine. If they will see what has been done in the town of Windsor at Fort Edward by allowing physical training in the good free air of Nova Scotia, they will realize that that is a great deal better than having Colonel Edwards or some of the historic commiteee come from Ottawa and do a lot of fancy work. I am going to oppose this appropriation unless I get a definite answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sure that I would almost take the word of the hon. gentleman for the preservation of child life in Windsor. All the hon. gentleman need do is for him and his friends to go to the municipality, and surely the municipal authorities will be public-spirited enough to back up a project of this kind. He is not asking for any money from them; he is not asking for any assistance in a financial way. Surely they will be quite willing to join him in the matter. That is all I ask. We ask for no money; we will give them all the ground except the small quantity required for the purposes of the site, to utilize as they see fit, to make toboggan slides or skating rinks, or ski-ing places, or any mortal thing they wish. But as I pointed out to him before, not that I have any objection to him or his associates, I must be definite that we must have the municipality behind all projects of this kind. Let me give the committee an instance in Saskatchewan. After I came into office in this government, I found, with the best intentions in the world, three gentlemen had got possession of the shore line in a certain locality. The municipality had a portion of it. When the municipality wished to extend, they found that these three gentlemen held privileges there, and we had a great deal of difficulty in getting them to surrender to the municipality. It is only because I am more insistent than the hon. gentleman that child life and the playgrounds be protected, that I am asking that the municipality be behind the project.

With all due deference
to the minister, I beg to say that applications were made in the past, and through too much red tape in his department, for which I do not blame him, because it was prior to his administration, the people could not get their request granted. It seems that a few people in Ottawa, who happen to have some high-falutin ideas of what is right and wrong, are going to be allowed to rule the whole country. Now, what is good in Saskatchewan is not necessarily good in Nova Scotia; for example, my hon. friend would not have many 
supporters in the latter province. Applications have been made time and again from the province of Nova Scotia to have Fort Edward in the town of Windsor converted into a public playground, and we are told to-day that we must go to the municipality. The minister does not know our conditions. We have several, municipalities in my county; at least, there are two municipalities, East Hants and West Hants', together with the corporation of the town of Windsor and the corporation of Hantsport. The minister does not know how we run things there, nor have his officials any idea of our conditions. I say this with all respect to the minister. But we do not wish to have a few people in Ottawa think that they can drive things down our throat. Whether the minister gives it or not, I say that there are twenty-eight or twenty-nine acres in the heart of the town of Windsor that can be converted to the purpose proposed; a fence can be placed around the old block house of the fort so that the children might have a playground. I can name persons in the town who are in favour of this scheme. Mr. H. W. Sangster, an opponent of mine who ran in the election, and my hon. friend Dr. Baxter, from St. John, are interested in it. The latter gentleman has been very much interested in the matter, because he has children, as I have also. His children, however, are grown-up while mine are not; and speaking in behalf of those similarly circumstanced, I say that we should not be held down by rigid rules and regulations, drawn up by people sitting in offices in Ottawa, which shall deprive us of this right to which we are entitled. I do not want to see any vote passed to-night that will provide for the appointment of certain officials in Ottawa who do not know anything about our local conditions, to prevent us from having a proper request granted.

Will the minister explain
the very large increase in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The increase of $284,480 is made up of a variety of items. On August 1, 1923, the Bankhead Mines plant which has supplied electric current for Banff will close down and the department has to install an electric plant. There is an item of $150,000 for this purpose. All these expenditures, I might explain, are charged, rightly or wrongly, to revenue account. There is no capitalized expenditure; the system is "pay as you go." Sanitary conditions at Canmore, a town in the Banff park, are bad on account of polluted wells. It is' proposed to expend $17,000 there to meet the situation. The Canadian National Railway is carrying on an extensive campaign to attract tourist business

Supply-Interior
to Jasper Park and the department is cooperating by proceeding with development work which will make Jasper's attractions accessible. The new road programme provides for an increase of $45,750. There is also an item of $5,000 to build a golf course at Jasper. The commercial value of a tourist naturally is increased by lengthening his stay, and experience has shown that a golf course is very effective in this connection. It is expected that 1,000 buffalo will be slaughtered at Buffalo park next winter. An appropriation of $13,000 is being made to provide suitable buildings for the slaughtering operations and the care of the meat. The range at Buffalo park is now not equal to the demand on it in consequence of the increase in the buffalo. It is proposed to expend $6,000 fencing in additional lands now belonging to the park.
The range at Elk Island has also become too limited for the buffalo, elk and moose herds there. An extension of the park into the Cooking Lake Forest Reserve has been arranged for. This will require 22 miles of fencing and, with fireguards, and so forth, will cost about $40,000.
Waterton Lakes park is visited by very large numbers of campers, chiefly Canadians from Alberta. It is proposed to spend $11,500 on a water supply for the townsite and campsites and to improve conditions at the campsites. There are now so many visitors there that it is feared the water in the lake may at any time become contaminated and unfit for drinking.

At Banff the Canadian Pacific Railway has a most profitable tourist traffic, largely because of its hotel. The fact has sometimes struck me, when I have visited the place, that the park is maintained in no small degree for the benefit of the company, who have been able to erect this large hotel on the line of the railway. What tax is the Canadian Pacific Railway paying for this great privilege?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The administration of a municipality such as Banff is rather difficult, and we have to co-operate largely with the provincial authoritites. So far there has been no power of taxation; we apply the licensing system to the lots which are practically all on the same basis. We have no power to tax but we charge water rates, light rates and so forth. [DOT] That is a matter in regard to which we shall endeavour to come to an arrangement with the provincial government.

I suggest that since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is
exploring new fields of taxation there is one that lies close at hand there. I do not know what the profits are from that great hotel, but I do know that there is a very heavy tourist traffic there, and an immense amount of advertising of the place is carried on throughout the whole world. We have spent an enormous sum on the park, which is maintained largely for the benefit of that hotel. There are similar hotels in the vicinity and a certain number of people travel by motor car to the park. But on the whole this large corporation is the chief beneficiary, and it seems to me we have a perfect right to see that a certain part of the revenue comes back to the state.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have the Banff park in fairly good condition, and I think that in order to direct traffic along the Canadian National line we should begin to make expenditures in the parks through which our own railways run. I do not know that the rates the hotel charges are unreasonable, but even the rates they charge tourists will pay them very handsome profits on the hotel investment. Of course the park is a great attraction for tourists and brings business to the railway.
If they do not get it directly out of the hotel they get it indirectly out of the railway.
It was stated that the item included a sum for providing an electric light plant at Banff. Was that work let by tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The excavation and the general labouring work has been carried on by day labour under the supervision of our own engineers at the park, but all the plant has been purchased by tender.

Will the minister kindly answer my question as to whether or not if the people desire to have a park for the children at Fort Edward, that they shall have authority to enclose the ground, apart from the historic portion, on making proper representations to the minister without reference to the officials in his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I promise my hon. friend that if he will have the mayor of Windsor come to me as the official representative of the town the whole matter will be settled in five minutes.
You will grant us that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
