Mr. MaeLEAN (Prince, P.E.I.): The estimates we are passing to-night are largely for the western provinces. Sometimes we in the East wonder a little at the large expenditures on this account, but we understand that the natural resources of the three prairie provinces have not yet been handed over to the provincial authorities, and therefore the Dominion government is under obligation to take care of certain works. However, I hope when the time comes for these natural resources to be turned over to the prairie provinces the eastern provinces will receive something in return, if not by way of compensation for our equity in those natural resources, at least something in lieu of the expenditures made by the federal government from time to time.
We have a lot of pretty little sites in the Maritime provinces where public parks could be laid out to which a large tourist traffic might be attracted, thus benefiting both the province itself and the Canadian National Railway. A large number of people of this beautiful city come down in the summer time to our seaside resorts,, and I believe that a little government assistance towards the laying out and beautifying of parks, such as has been done in other places, would greatly increase our tourist traffic. I hope the minister in looking over the different provinces will not pass by the "little island province" down by the sea.

I am rather amazed at the suggestion made by the last speaker. If he will examine the Estimates I think he will find that the West has considerable ground for grievance in so far as expenditures in western Canada are concerned as compared with those in eastern Canada. The expenditure in this particular case of $150,000 on an electric lighting plant for the town of Banff is an absolute necessity.
Why do they not go to the local government?

The minister has already indicated that by reason of the failure of the government to give the people there municipal powers, they cannot themselves function as a municipality at all; they have not the necessary legislative jurisdiction.
Why do they not go to the local government?

It is not a question of going to the local government. These lands are reserved by the Dominion government as a national park, and the local government have no jurisdiction. But that is not what I want

to speak about for the moment. An electric lighting plant is an absolute necessity owing to the fact that the old plant has been closed down. You cannot leave the people in darkness. According to the last census Banff has a population of something over two thousand, and during the tourist season I am sure it must be increased by several thousands more. An adequate lighting plant must be maintained for the convenience of these people. I regret the minister did not see fit to have the work done by tender. I think it would have been desirable to call for tenders, with the stipulation that the all-the-year-round inhabitants of the town of Banff and the neighbourhood should be given an opportunity to do whatever work they could handle. I think that would have been desirable because in the winter time the people are to a large extent isolated from other sections of the country.
The minister has suggested a very interesting problem-the municipal government of these small towns within the park area. As I said before, this land was reserved some thirty or forty years ago for a national park. The communities within the park area have no authority to organize themselves in the regular way. I think the late administration formulated a policy by which a considerable measure of local government was granted to these people, which is desirable, and the policy has been continued by this government. I think the power of the local authorities should be enlarged to the fullest possible extent. I do not know any method of governing people satisfactorily other than by letting them govern themselves. Certainly they should not be governed from Ottawa in connection wtih their local affairs. It is true that under some arrangement-I do not know how it is worked-these people have a right to tax themselves for school purposes. However, I think that in regard to municipal government they should be given the widest possible latitude in order that they may attend effectively to their own local affairs.
There is one other suggestion I want to make. I agree with the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) that we have altogether too much government from Ottawa. Undoubtedly the tendency during- the next few years is going to be towards decentralization in government.
dear, hear.

I think the Parks Commissioner should be located out in western Canada where the main area of the national parks is situated. Hon. members may be

Supply-Interior
surprised to know that of the national parks and historic sites in Canada, comprising altogether approximately eight thousand square miles, only one hundred and sixty
acres are located in eastern Canada, these being composed largely of historic sites such as that indicated by the hon. member for Hants. In the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia considerably over seven thousand nine hundred square miles of our national parks are situated. I see no reason why the Parks Commissioner whose duty it is to superintend these parks should not be located at a convenient spot-probably the town of Banff- where he can admininster these vast areas with the least possible difficulty, instead of being detained down in the city of Ottawa far from his work and unable to keep in immediate touch with it. For that reason it is desirable that the Parks Commissioner should be located there. With regard to the historic sites, I think there is much in what the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Mar-tell) says. Perhaps the Quebec Battlefields Commission could take them over, or some special commission might be created in eastern Canada to look after these matters which, though very important, are of comparatively minor importance from the point of view of administration. I therefore suggest to the minister, as I have previously suggested in the House, that the Commisisoner of Parks-and I say now, even in his presence, that he is a very competent official, one who is extremely anxious to work out this park situation to the greatest possible advantage to the people of Canada-should be located in a spot which is central and which is close to his work. There is one other matter that I want to draw to the attention of the committee at this time, namely, the completion this year of what :s known as the Banff-Windermere highway. This is an event not only of national but of international importance. The completion of this highway, the construction of which was commenced under the late government through an agreement with the province of British Columbia, completes what is known as the circle tour. One may start by motor, on foot, or by carriage if he likes, from the city of Calgary and go to Banff; proceeding thence through the Rocky mountains by way of Vermilion pass, and down to Windermere, thence south almost to the boundary, returning by way of Crowsnest pass, if he so desires, in the southern part of the province, to Macleod, and then north again to Calgary, a distance, I think, of some 567 miles. That route is not only of interest to the people of Alberta and British Columbia; it gives many
people an opportunity to traverse this country and get in touch with the great highways of the United States. One can commence, we will say, at the town of Banff, can proceed practically to the Mexican boundary, over the very best of highways, and can then return by an altogether different course through Colorado canyon and the American parks in the northwestern United States, returning thence to the point of commencement.
Will he ever come back?

I am sure many will. But it is not only that it gives an opportunity for Canadians to travel over this vast area of Canada and the United States, but, what is of infinitely greater importance, it gives a large number of American tourists an opportunity to traverse the Canadian Rockies by way of the circle tour. There have been numerous inquiries-I have no doubt that the Parks branch have also received them without number-as to the time of the completion of that highway.
How much will that highway cost and in whose constituency is it situated?

My hon. friend will be glad to know that a considerable part of it runs through the constituency of the
10 p.m. Minister of Public Works (Mr. ICing); part of it runs through the constituency of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), and a comparatively small portion of it runs through the constituency of West Calgary. But I may tell my hon. friend for his information that perhaps before he was born I was familiar with the situation at Banff. I have watched the development of the national park for over thirty years, and I am tremendously interested in the completion of this project. It is a great work; it has been splendidly carried out, and it is going to attract tourists not by hundreds, not by thousands, but by tens of thousands to the great national recreation ground of Canada. I am sure that the result will not only be beneficial to the Canadian people but it will create in the United States a tremendous interest in Canada which will be followed, I hope, by a very large immigration into various parts at least, of our western country. Our national parks-and I include in that not only the Banff National Park but also Jasper Park and others-constitute one of the greatest heritages of Canadians to-day. Some who are familiar with the facts have pointed out that the Rocky
Supply-Interior

mountain districts constitute ten Switzerlands rolled into one. There is not a member of this House who can visualize the possibilities of these parks within, say, the next fifty years; one hesitates even to suggest those possibilities. There is one thing about a park; man may harness and destroy waterfalls and natural attractions of every character, but when parks are preserved the people have the privilege of enjoying them, and they are not destroyed; they remain there. So I say that the opening of the Banff-Windermere highway on the twentieth, I believe, of this month, is a matter of very great national importance. I regret that the House will be sitting at that time; for there are many who urge that one of the first duties of members of parliament should be to travel from one end of this country to the other. I think it should be done; it is in the national interest that it should be done. It would result in the elimination of much of the sectionalism and provincialism with which members are sometimes charged, and I could not possibly think of a better occasion for hon. members to visit western Canada than at this particular time, when they may traverse at least the small circle tour within the confines of Canada. I simply want to say this, Mr. Chairman, because I think hon. members should get some idea of what has been done, of what these parks are, and of what are their possibilities, not only for the present but, I trust, in the not too far distant future.
Is anything provided for the improvement of this route by its being connected up through the Waterton park region?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know the ground so well that I appreciate what my hon. friend is interested in. It is a matter primarily for the province, and Mr. Greenfield has given his promise that it will be attended to this year.

I want to call the attention of the committee to that portion of this tourist route, because it is one of very great interest to my constituency and will in time, I believe, become of very great interest to the people of Canada generally. A great many tourists go through our part of the country every year, especially from the western states of the union. We have a great many things there that might well claim the tourist's attention. We have Waterton Lakes and its park, in the first place, which is as beautiful a bit of scenery,
I think, as can be found anywhere in Canada. Then we have other things which lend peculiar

interest to that part of the country. One of the things which attracts tourists to that district is the great Mormon temple that has been built during the last few years at Cards-ton, near the place where I live. That magnificent building probably attracts more of the attention of tourists than any	other building	in	the West;
they flock there by the thousands. At the present time the park-the little park surrounding that building-is being beautified by the planting of trees and shrubs and is becoming, I think, one of the nicest spots in the entire West. Besides that we have to show to the people journeying through that part of the country the results of the irrigation projects which are going on there and to which I referred a little while ago. We want people to go through that district and see what can be done by artificial methods of providing water. We want them to see our splendid fields of alfalfa, of timothy, and of forage of all kinds, our well equipped creameries and fine herds of cattle. We have all these things to interest tourists, and to bring money,->
ready money-into the western part of panada. I hope that the minister in providing for these highways-tourist highways especially,-will see that that south-western corner of Alberta is not neglected, for I feel that it has not been sufficiently advertised in Canada, and that it is a part of the Dominion to which the eastern residents of this country might well direct their attention.
The member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) has called attention to something which particularly interests me, and that is the necessity of the East and the West coming together more frequently, thereby causing the various sections of this country to understand one another's problems. Since I came down here last year I have been taken on three trips in eastern Canada through the generosity of different organizations, boards of trade, harbour commissioners, and other bodies of that kind, and it has opened my eyes to many things of importance which the farmer, especially the western farmer is wont to overlook. Now, in turn we want you people of the East, who are interested in your manufac luring enterprises, interested in a different class of enterprises to what we are in the West to return those visits, to come to the Weot and glean a thorough understanding of our problems. I believe that by such an interchange of visits we shall gradually knit this country more and more into a complete whole and that as a result we shall work together in greater harmony and with a better understanding

The minister tells us that he proposes to slaughter a thousand buffalo and that he is going to put up a plant for the purpose. What is going to be done with the carcases?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Many of the animals that are being slaughtered are animals that were purchased when the herd was first started at Wainwright and consequently are of mature age. We intend to make most of the meat into pemmican. But my hon. friend will readily understand there is only a limited demand for the sale of that product. It can be sold in the northern country, and we have some thought of trying to introduce it into the navy where meats have to be stored-in other words it may, perhaps, take the place of corned beef on shipboard.
That is a land force now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not immediately.
My hon. friend cannot have reference to the Canadian navy because that is always ashore.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have reference to the British navy. As we get to the period when we will slaughter the younger animals the meat will undoubtedly sell very rapidly. The animals are increasing in that park reserve now at the rate of approximately
2,000	a year so that it is beginning to be a serious problem to provide pasturage for feeding. They are also increasing in the Lamont park, where the first buffalo were placed, and in the north. Although we have not accurate figures we think there are in the neighbourhood of 2,000 head at least in the Hay river district on the Mackenzie. We have set aside a park area there, appointed rangers, and propose to take care of these buffalo because they may prove a very important factor in the future in feeding the Indians if that becomes necessary. They are doing very well. They are much larger than when they are kept in a confined area, and seem to be very healthy. Since the Eskimo has been armed he is beginning to shoot the caribou which are so numerous in the north country. Not only that but he is beginning to shoot the seal which heretofore he has always captured. Indeed, I think it was a mistake to arm him because his food supply may become a problem in the very near future. The Indian in the Northwest Territories is not a very energetic individual, in fact he is a very poor hunter, and we must provide for the possibility of having to take care of the Indian, perhaps even in the near future-that is to
conserve a food supply for him. We hope this herd of buffalo will increase very rapidly in that country if given reasonable protection. That we propose to do by having herders riding in the area in which those animals are ranging. I may say that we have met one rather serious difficulty that has induced us, perhaps, to slaughter a little more rapidly than we first intended. In the animals we slaughtered this year we found 'traces of tuberculosis, some of it not serious, some rather serious, some of it in the tongue. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture could explain the operations of this disease very much better than I can but, as hon. gentlemen know sometimes after its inception it heals over. That is the case in connection with the buffalo. We cannot catch them and inoculate them, we cannot treat them the same as we do cattle, and that is rather a serious feature of the situation. We are hoping, however, that it will not be as serious a proposition as it appeared to be after the slaughtering of 160 or 180 head this year.
Do you blame the cattalo for the introduction of tuberculosis?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Possibly it developed by reason of what I have told my hon. friend. There were animals in which it appeared that were thought to have been cured. The disease developed at the root of the tongue. I cannot describe the origin and progress of this disease in technical terms, I can only speak of it as a layman. These animals must have been infected several years ago. The experiment carried on with the cattalo cannot be blamed for the infection of the herd. The veterinary seems to think that the herd is getting entirely too numerous.

As the minister needs funds very badly he will be very glad to know that buffalo heads are worth quite a sum of money. I understood there had been a sale at auction some time ago, and that prices as high as $500 had been paid for good buffalo heads. Is that correct?

We propose to offer them for sale. We propose to advertise very extensively in Great Britain. It was proposed that we should have an exhibit at the carnival in Montreal this winter, but we did not carry it out. The intention is	to advertise extensively	in	the UnitedStates, both the hides and	robes, in	order
to secure buyers for them. If the herd continues to increase, and we are slaughtering
2,000	a year, the number will remain about normal. If we had 5,000 head in the Buffalo park, I think it would be all we are entitled to	have in that enclosure,	to	keep	themhealthy. We would need to sell between 1,500 and 2,000 a year, and possibly the price of	robes and heads would	go	down	very
rapidly, if those large numbers were put on the market, but they have been very valuable.
What has become of the electric plant at Calgary, now going out of existence? Why can the government not operate that? They could easily obtain it. It cannot be worth anything to the owners.

and cows?

speechtext: All bulls.

Are they troubled with
actinomycosis, or lumpy jaw?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

lumpy jaw.

Do you follow the ordinary plan in feeding range cattle, of putting the hay on the ground?
Mr. STEW7ART (Argenteuil):	Yes.

Unless the ground is frequently changed, that is one of the causes of range cattle becoming infected with tuberculosis. A high piece of ground is selected on account of its dryness, and they continue to feed hay on the same ground. The ground becoming foul, when there is a thaw the hay gets infected from the moist ground, and the animals become infected through the intestinal tract, and that is one reason why these animals living in the open air are affected to a considerable extent with tuberculosis. What results have been derived from the treatment of infected animals?
Mr. STEW7ART (Argenteuil): I could not give the hon. member that information. The Department of Agriculture is in charge of that.

The discussion on the
national parks has taken a somewhat wide range, and possibly I may be permitted to detain the House a moment to state that in Truro, my own town,-and if this is out of order I may say I am not asking for anything-
You are rather out of order, if you do not want anything.

The irregularity may last a moment. We have a small park there, and it is the most beautiful inland park east of Stanley park in British Columbia. It is in a wooded ravine and gorge in which there are a never-failing brook and falls of dignified proportion and rare beauty called the Joe Howe Falls, after our great orator of earlier days. He had visited those falls frequently and he had committed to print some of his beautifully descriptive language concerning those falls. This park is almost immediately adjoining the depot of the Canadian National Railway, and if any of my hon. friends happen to be down that way, I would bespeak that they try to devote an hour or two, to meandering through the bewitching walks of that park, and when I meet them again I shall not be afraid to repeat my protestation that this is the most beautiful natural park east of Stanley park in British Columbia. It is maintained under a local board of trustees in conjunction with the local municipal authority. In happier financial years a request was unsuccessfully made to the federal government for some grant for the further support and care of this park. During the present need of national economy I am not meantime repeating the request. But I hope that all who may henceforth see Truro will treat themselves to a stroll in this park: and they will agree that I have not told half the truth.

Supply-Interior

I can remember very well, when we had the park estimates, meeting some pretty vigorous objections to their size and to their character, and the criticism made that every principle of economy was being sacrificed, the depleted treasury being bled and the country's money being wasted. I am going to ask my hon. friend for a little serious consideration of this vote tonight. I want to point out to him that for the year 1921-22, when accusations of this character were made against us, the vote for these parks amounted to $800,000, while the vote for the parks to-day amounts to $1,250,980; that in a short period those expenses which at one time were described as being so high and extravagant, have been increased under this administration over 50 per cent. I am going to ask the minister to let us have the full details of this vote, showing us where this money is going. The parks are not running away. I do not know that in any year any finance minister of Canada had more reason for concern in connection with extravagant expenditure than my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has this year, when he is budgeting for a direct deficit. Can my- hon. friend the Minister of the Interior not have a little consideration for the Finance Minister, who, after all, I suppose, is more deeply interested in this question than any of us. We have only one thing given us to-day in connection with the so-called emergency expense payments that have to be made, and that is that plant which has been referred to. That is the only matter of emergency that I have heard of so far, and that one little matter of emergency amounts to $162,000, if I heard my hon. friend correctly. Now what else is there? What else is there to-day of immediate necessity that was not present in the year 1921-22, when we got along with $800,000? There were reasons why money was spent then that do not obtain to-day. The departmental officers will recollect very well that work was entered upon the year after the war for the express purpose of giving employment when employment was so badly needed-I am not sure it was 1920-21 or 1921-22, I think it was the former year-when Governor General's warrants were issued just for the purpose of doing work which, although it was proper work, could have been postponed, were it not for the question of unemployment. Some of the roads were gone on with at that time, having regard to that issue, and bridges were undertaken. None of those matters is pressing my hon. friend to-day. We hear protestations of economy. I would like the minister to show
us exactly how those protestations work out, with an increase of over fifty per cent in a two-year period.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the year the hon. member mentions, the total expenditure was $966,328, instead of the $800,000 mentioned by him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am giving my hon. friend the expenditure.

That is the only reason why the appropriation was increased, and my hon. friend will find, I think, that my statement is correct-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not disputing it.

-that the extra amount over the $800,000 represented commitments which were taken up for the purpose of relieving a very pressing need, having regard to the unemployment situation. Apart from that there is the $800,000 appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to ask for the whole of the items?
Yes. Perhaps it would save time if we were to let the item stand and go on with the other items.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would
rather give my hon. friend the items and be done with it.

I would suggest to my hon. friend that the quickest thing to do would be to let us have a little memorandum on that without wasting the time of the committee now. The minister has several other items to go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have the memorandum here. I will give my hon. friend the total amount spent.

Supply-Interior

For the three years under consideration. Perhaps we would make better headway in this manner. This matter was drawn to my attention by my leader who knows much more about it than I do, and I know he wants to speak on it anyway. Perhaps time will be saved if this item is allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would be glad, if there is any information I can get, if the hon. member would give me a statement
I will see the officials afterwards and give them a statement so that there need be no delay.
What is the policy of the government regarding the granting of leases of water-powers in national parks?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There has been only one lease granted, that.is the grant to the Calgary Power Company. They are making application for increased power, and I announced before six o'clock that the matter had not been settled. The application has oeen before us for some considerable time. They asked for increased power in lake Minnewanka, and we have definitely refused +hat. They subsequently asked for power on the Spray lakes; the matter has been given consideration, and it will be given further consideration on Tuesday evening when officials of the department and one or two of the ministers are to hear representations from the power company in connection with the matter.
Is this the company that has made application for permission to construct a dam somewhere near Banff in the national park?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I understand there is no
settled policy yet by the government regarding the general matter of granting waterpower leases in national parks. I know many people are very much interested in this question, and I think most of them take the view that water-powers in these parks should not be leased to any parties, although one *was granted near Banff some years ago. I was just trying to find out, if possible, what

the policy of the government was. I sincerely hope, if the government have no settled policy, they will decide that the water-powers in these parks should not be leased. It seems to me that, in the national parks at any rate, these water-powers should be kept for the people. In fact, I hope in most cases, for a good many years to come, it will not be necessary to interfere with the natural beauty. If these water-powers at least in the national parks, are ever to be harnessed, that certainly should be done under the control of the people. I would like to impress upon the committee that I think the people of the country generally are very strongly in support of such a policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the
province of Alberta particularly, most of the heads of streams will be in park property or properties of the Crown, and to say definitely that at no time under no consideration will you grant leases for power purposes, will be, perhaps, going a long distance. I agree thoroughly with my hon. friend that the scenic beauty, particularly within the area of national parks used by tourists and others, should be preserved. I may say to my hon. friend who has just spoken in such high terms of the country from which he comes, the Waterton lake area which is a park area, that the people there are very anxious to utilize that for irrigation purposes, and this will be exactly on a par with the application of the power company. There are many aspects to this question. The United States government, however, who have given this matter very considerable attention, have adopted the principle as far as possible to conserve the natural beauty and to refuse applicants for power sites within the boundaries of their parks.

I was hoping the minister
would give us the opinion that the policy of the government in that particular case would follow the policy of the United States government. As regards the case he mentions of the Waterton lakes, I think just as many people are opposed to the using of Waterton lakes as an irrigation reservoir as there are who are in favour of that proposition. I do not want to go into that at all. I hope the minister will see that the water-powers in our parks are preserved.
I understand that this item stands.
Why does it have to stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

Engraving, lithographing, printing, and preparation of maps, plans reports and kindred publications of the Dominion, including salaries and necessary materials for same, etc., $120,700.
What is the reason for this increase of $15,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have not had a sufficient amount to meet the demand for the maps which are now very widely used. We do not send these maps out indiscriminately; we simply supply them on demand; but they are used very largely throughout Canada, the United States and elsewhere and are of immense advantage in advertising our national resources. I believe that they also play an important part in inducing capital to come to Canada. That is why I am asking for the increase.
Does the grant cover all maps issued by the government, or are there some maps issued by other departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It does not include the maps of all the departments, but I think I am safe in saying that 95 per cent of the maps that go out from the government service come from the Interior department.
Are these maps furnished free on application to anyone in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

All the

clerks in other departments who are looking after the lands that should come under this department being transferred to the Department of Interior?

To satisfy the claims of the half-breeds of the Mackenzie River District, N.W.T., $42,240.

item.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
These claims arise out of the treaty settlement with the Indians of the north. On former occasions hon. members will recall that half-breeds who happened to be on the reserve were given scrip, not being entitled to treaty money. Under the arrangement the late Mr. Conroy made when in the north country he proposed to settle one hundred and fifty halfbreed claims by giving them $240 apiece. I am inclined to think that is a good arrangement, for we have always had complaints regarding the transfer of half-breed scrip. I believe my hon. friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) is still anxious to probe claims arising out of such transfers. On this

occasion Mr. Conroy recommended a settlement in cash.
Just a straight cash grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, of $240 per head. Thirty-six claims have been submitted for further investigation to ascertain whether they are entitled to consideration. One hundred and forty claims have been settled, representing a cash payment of $33,600, and thirty-six claims outstanding will require another $8,640, making a total of $42,240.
How is it that parties entitled to payment were not settled with in 1900?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot tell my hon. friend, but these matters always entail some considerable time to make sure the men are entitled to consideration.

speechtext: My record goes back to the inception of the relief in 1876. Do settlers who
break up school lands make application to the minister's department for seed grain advances?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That has been rather a vexed question, and I had to deal with it in the province of Alberta. The provincial authorities found, as far as I know, that they could not advance seed grain in such cases; the federal authorities did not think they were entitled to do so either. There is not very much security on school lands for the advance of seed grain. I am now informed that the federal government never makes these advances to purchasers of school lands.

Supply-Interior

I have a letter under my hand from the reeve of a municipality in my district in regard to school lands that are sold and brought under cultivation by the purchaser and then allowed to revert to the Crown. Possibly a short extract will explain the point I wish to direct attention to. In this letter dated March 27th last the writer says, in part:
Quite recently a purchaser of school lands in our municipality has turned these lands back to the Crown and received his clearance papers. He owes the municipality in taxes about $400. He had at least two thousand bushels of wheat on these lands this year, and had the council been notified that the lands were reverting back to the Crown we could have collected by distraint. As well as losing the taxes, we are now confronted with the expense of destroying noxious weeds on these lands without any hope of recovery.
The point this gentleman wishes brought to the attention of the department is that the municipality should be notified when school lands revert to the Crown. Would it not be possible for the Department of the Interior to adopt a certain fixed policy so that when any school lands are about to revert to the Crown they would notify the rural municipality? Then in such a case as this letter refers to the municipality might take action in time to recover the taxes. I know of another case in my locality where the taxes amoimt to $2,800 on a quarter section which reverted to the Crown. These taxes are lost to the municipality. Would it not be possible to notify the municipal officials prior to the cancellation of any contract for school lands?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There would be no objection if it were possible, but we only know of the cancellation when the surrender is sent in. There may be very rare [DOT]cases in which we have notification of intention to abandon, but in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the first notification we have is the notice that the purchaser has decided to abandon. By that time any notification to the municipality would not be of very much value.
Does that mean that the owner of the land would notify the department and then immediately leave?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid he does very frequently. In some cases where they are owners of other land in the municipality of course there is a remedy. But where they leave the municipality we seldom get notification of their intention to abandon until they have moved away.

Can a settler grow
2.000	bushels of wheat, get the proceeds from that, tell the department he is leaving, and then leave the land without making a payment?	'

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course we would have the right of ordinary action against him.
But if he is gone, what then?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the difficulty. If we proceed to seize his crop there would be a hue and a cry-I am assuming now he was in arrears. The usual procedure is to notify the purchaser when payments of principal or interest are due, and we expect these to be forwarded. If they are not forwarded, it is seldom that we take any drastic action against the purchaser. Naturally, if he decided to relinquish he would not leave very many of his assets around on which we might recover.
Is there any local supervision of the owners of these lands at the crop threshing time?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
It is left entirely to the individual to make the payment to the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Yes.

speechtext: I could not say that.

Oh, no, I
cannot say to that. There would be some of it not collectible.

speechtext: It would be difficult to segregate the amounts-what is paid to the banks, and what are the travelling expenses of the collectors and their salaries. However, we can furnish the hon. member with the information.

speechtext:
Yes.
IMr. C. A. Stewart.]

speechtext: Yes, that is the total amount.

I have in mind one
municipality that has assumed an indebtedness in this connection of some $70,000 or $75,000, and they are still paying interest on that loan in addition to the regular .municipal loan. speechtext: There is an arrangement between the federal and the provincial governments under which they will ultimately share in the loss that may accrue. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, it is
a burden they themselves assumed. A bond issue was undertaken to relieve the municipality-to relieve them not of
11 p.m. ultimate payment, but of the burden of constantly renewing a note at the bank.

Does that mean
that the municipality eventually has to pay back all the amount?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes.

In the district to which I refer a great many persons who got loans of from $800 to $1,000 or $1,500 have left the municipality. Is it the intention of the department to compel the local unit to pay the full amount of the loan regardless of that condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I say,
the municipalities took that responsibility on themselves. They were responsible for the loan, and I do not see how either the provincial or the federal government could come to their rescue by assuming a liability which is clearly the liability of the municipality.

This particular unit to which I refer is under the impression that

Supply-Interior
the provincial and Dominion governments . are going to assume the liability, and they are waiting for them to take steps to that end.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not heard of any steps of that kind being proposed.

I should just like to say that I went through an experience thirty years ago in connection with the handing out of seed grain and because the government guaranteed the payment of debentures individual farmers got it into their heads that the government were advancing the money and went into debt. Consequently the debt is one belonging to the municipality. The same thing has been happening year after year, I know that from personal experience in the province of Manitoba, so that in that province the municipalities will not make advances in connection with seed grain any more. Before I sit down I should like to ask if all this money was advanced upon loan from the Dominion government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I think the system has prevailed for the past seven or eight years.

What about the 1876 loan?
I cannot make that out; it puzzles me, a little.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know what was done.
Are the seed grain transactions we are discussing entirely separate and distinct from the purchases made by the Seed Purchasing Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The latter are under the Department of Agriculture.

They are not included in
this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

I understood from the answer given by the minister to the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) that part of this money being voted is for relief given in the year 1914. If that is so I think the matter would stand close investigation. I think it absolutely wrong that municipalities should be shouldered with the debt incurred in the matter of granting relief. It was the result of that campaign because you can term it nothing else. The dried out areas in the West were supposed to be given relief. It was on what was expected to be the eve of an election and the relief extended far beyond the bounds of the dried out areas; it was granted to people
220J
- who were in no way in need of relief. Considerable relief was given to people in the municipality in which I live, and since that time we have come through much worse periods of stress. With respect to my own municipality all that an individual had to do was to get on the train, go up to a certain town on the line, make his own representations to the so-called relief officer who knew nothing whatever of the circumstances and come away with relief in the shape of an order on the stores in the district for groceries, flour or fuel. Now, why should a municipality be made to bear the expense of that relief?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are not responsible for it.
I understood the minister to say that in reply to a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are not sponsible only for the obligations they assumed themselves, not for any obligations assumed by the government to the homesteaders. Obligations were taken on in 1917, 1918 and 1919 by the municipalities themselves. When the government of the province and the government of the Dominion refused to go on with relief, the municipalities issued relief in their own names under municipal officers. That is the relief I was discussing with my hon. friend from Kindersley.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Amount required to provide relief by way of necessary supplies of food, clothing, fuel etc., also fodder for animals to needy settlers of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan by co-operation and agreement with the provincial governments or otherwise, and under regulations to be made by the Governor in Council, $125,000.

Would the minister tell us
what was spent of the amount voted last year under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We spent.
$232,250 out of what was voted last year.

If grants have been made for this purpose to other provinces I should like to know why the minister could not extend any assistance to settlers in the Nicola valley in British Columbia. The minister was out there last year and he learned for himself that the Nicola valley was practically cleaned out owing to depredations by grasshoppers. The minister will remember that we applied for some assistance but were turned down. Now, am I to understand that fodder was supplied to other provinces and not to British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The assistance only applied to homesteaders or people
Supply-Interior

on Crown lands in any of the western provinces. I do not suppose my hon. friend's representations would come under that category. Some of the settlers would be on lands owned by the province but in most of the cases the lands would be privately owned and under municipal organization, would they not?
There are some under the provinces and some in the railway belt. There are quite a number of homesteaders there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
recollect an application being turned down where it was warranted. This was paid out generally by the provincial government and the Dominion. I cannot recollect any application coming from the homesteaders in the Nicola valley.
The minister surely remembers being out there, and that the provincial government were prepared to stand their part of the expense.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We usually leave the matter to them but, of course, we are prepared to co-operate with them.
Yes, but if the Dominion government was spending money in other provinces it certainly should have spent some in the Nicola valley.
I think my hon. friend from British Columbia does not understand the circumstances. In British Columbia the government own and control the lands in that province.

Not in the railway belt.
The Dominion owns the railway belt.

Then I do not see any
reason why the same treatment should not have been extended to settlers on Crown lands there as was extended in the case of other provinces.

There may be another
reason. It is very seldom justifiable to accord relief where there has only been a loss of one crop. In many districts in Saskatchewan and Alberta the settlers lost four crops in succession. I do not know whether the conditions are the same in the valley to which my hon. friend (Mr. McBride) has referred. If so I do not see why they should not have received the same relief. However, that was the situation in the prairie provinces.

Is it not a fact that
part of this relief work had to be done through an arrangement with the provincial governments?
[Mr. C. A. Stewartll	I

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Two of the provincial governments entered into that arrangement whilst other provincial governments did not.

We could not very
well have refused to enter into an arrangement with the province of British Columbia had they so desired it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
what I say. It was a matter in the first place of the provincial government entering into the arrangement we have now.

I should like to
understand whether this is being done as charity to the farmers out in Alberta or whether it is a case of granting credit and taking a lien?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a loan.

Last year the appropriation was $325,000 and the minister has said that $232,250 was spent. This year the appropriation is $125,000. I presume the expenditure will be considerably less. Is that an indication of the general prosperity of Alberta and Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We cannot form any definite opinion of the requests. Of course, they come from the provincial government. They assume the responsibility of making advances and we become responsible for our share of them. So far as I know the Alberta government have done nothing in that line, or very little, and the government of the province of Saskatchewan have been exceedingly careful. I think the estimate of $125,000 will meet the case.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Graham the House adjourned at 11.15 p.m.
Tuesday, June 5, 1923
